Let $S$ be locally Noetherian and universally catenary with dimension function $\delta:S\to\mathbf Z$. For any $S$-scheme $T$ locally of finite type, use $\delta_T(t)=\delta(f(t))+\operatorname{trdeg}_{\kappa(f(t))}\kappa(t)$; for an integral closed subscheme $W\subset T$ write $\dim_\delta W=\delta_T(\eta_W)$.

The abelian group $Z_q(T)$ consists of locally finite integral linear combinations of integral closed subschemes of $\delta$-dimension $q$. For a closed subscheme $A$ of dimension at most $q$, let $[A]_q$ sum the $q$-dimensional components with multiplicities $\operatorname{length}_{\mathcal O_{T,\eta}}\mathcal O_{A,\eta}$. Let $\mathrm{CH}_q(T)$ be $Z_q(T)$ modulo rational equivalence generated by locally finite sums of principal Weil divisors on integral closed subschemes of $\delta$-dimension $q+1$.

For an invertible sheaf $\mathcal M$ on an integral scheme $W$ and a nonzero meromorphic section $u$, define $\operatorname{div}_{\mathcal M}(u)$ as the Weil divisor whose coefficients at codimension-one integral closed subschemes are orders of the local meromorphic function representing $u$ in a trivialization; at a height-one local domain $A$, for $a,b\in A\setminus\{0\}$, the order of $a/b$ is $\operatorname{length}_A(A/aA)-\operatorname{length}_A(A/bA)$. The class of this divisor in $\mathrm{CH}_{\dim_\delta(W)-1}(W)$ is $c_1(\mathcal M)\cap[W]$. For a global section $u$, $Z(u)$ is its scheme-theoretic zero locus.

For a flat morphism $h:T'\to T$ of relative dimension $r$, the pullback $h^*:Z_q(T)\to Z_{q+r}(T')$ sends $[W]$ to the cycle $[T'\times_T W]_{q+r}$ with scheme-theoretic multiplicities. It also induces a map on Chow groups.

Let $X$, $Y$ be locally of finite type over $S$. Assume $X$, $Y$
are integral and $n = \dim_\delta(Y)$.
Let $\mathcal{L}$ be an invertible $\mathcal{O}_Y$-module.
Let $f : X \to Y$ be a flat morphism of relative dimension $r$. Then
$$
f^*(c_1(\mathcal{L}) \cap [Y]) = c_1(f^*\mathcal{L}) \cap [X]
$$
in $\mathrm{CH}_{n + r - 1}(X)$.

We write $M[0]$ for a module concentrated in degree zero, $M[1]$ for a module in degree $-1$, $\otimes_A^{\mathbf L}$ for derived tensor product, and $\tau_{\geq -1}$ for the standard truncation in cohomological degrees at least $-1$. The module $\Omega_{B/A}$ is generated by symbols $db$ subject to additivity, the Leibniz rule, and $da=0$ for $a\in A$.

Let $A$ be a ring and let $P=A[S]$ be a polynomial ring over $A$. Let $M$ be a $(P, P)$-bimodule
over $A$. Given $m_s \in M$ for $s \in S$, there exists a unique
$A$-biderivation $\lambda : P \to M$ mapping $s$ to $m_s$ for $s \in S$.

records.title: Lemma — Dg hull

conclusions:
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a site and $\mathcal{F}$ a presheaf on $\mathcal{C}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The rule
$$
U \mapsto \mathcal{F}^+(U) :=
\colim_{\mathcal{U} \text{ covering of }U}
\check H^0(\mathcal{U}, \mathcal{F})
$$
is a presheaf. And the colimit is a directed one.
\item There is a canonical map of presheaves $\mathcal{F} \to \mathcal{F}^+$.
\item If $\mathcal{F}$ is a separated presheaf then $\mathcal{F}^+$ is a sheaf
and the map in (2) is injective.
\item $\mathcal{F}^+$ is a separated presheaf.
\item $\mathcal{F}^\# = (\mathcal{F}^+)^+$ is a sheaf, and the canonical
map induces a functorial isomorphism
$$
\Hom_{\textit{PSh}(\mathcal{C})}(\mathcal{F}, \mathcal{G}) =
\Hom_{\Sh(\mathcal{C})}(\mathcal{F}^\#, \mathcal{G})
$$
for any $\mathcal{G} \in \Sh(\mathcal{C})$.
\end{enumerate}
In the plus construction the colimit is filtered along covering refinements. A separated F has injective F→F^+ and F^+ is a sheaf; for arbitrary F, F^+ is separated and F^# is the universal associated sheaf. The Hom equivalence is the left-adjunction to inclusion Sh(C)→PSh(C).

records.title: Theorem — Sheafification

conclusions: $A \to B$ is an isomorphism
hypotheses:
Let $A \to B$ be ring map such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item $A \to B$ identifies local rings,
\item the topological spaces $\Spec(B)$, $\Spec(A)$ are w-local,
\item $\Spec(B) \to \Spec(A)$ is w-local, and
\item $\pi_0(\Spec(B)) \to \pi_0(\Spec(A))$ is bijective.
\end{enumerate}
records.statement:
**Source terminology (not extra hypotheses).** A **w-local** spectral space has closed set of closed points and every point specializes to a unique closed point; a w-local map between such spaces is spectral and sends closed points to closed points. A ring map $A\to B$ is a **local isomorphism** when near every prime of $B$ it induces an open immersion after inverting an element of $B$; it **identifies local rings** when $A_{q\cap A}\to B_q$ is an isomorphism for every prime $q$ of $B$.

Let $A \to B$ be ring map such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item $A \to B$ identifies local rings,
\item the topological spaces $\Spec(B)$, $\Spec(A)$ are w-local,
\item $\Spec(B) \to \Spec(A)$ is w-local, and
\item $\pi_0(\Spec(B)) \to \pi_0(\Spec(A))$ is bijective.
\end{enumerate}
Then $A \to B$ is an isomorphism

records.title: Lemma — Base change by space representable by space

conclusions: Triangle can be represented by a compatible inverse system of Deligne triangles on X.
hypotheses: Noetherian j:U→X, a bounded-coherent distinguished triangle on U.
records.statement: For a Noetherian scheme $X$, open immersion $j:U\hookrightarrow X$, and coherent bounded complex $\mathcal F^\bullet$ on $X$, choose a quasi-coherent ideal $\mathcal I\subset\mathcal O_X$ whose vanishing set is $X\setminus U$. Define $K_n$ as the bounded coherent *subcomplex* with terms $\mathcal I^n\mathcal F^q$ and differentials induced by those of $\mathcal F^\bullet$. The inverse system $(K_n)_{n\ge1}$, with maps induced by $\mathcal I^{n+1}\mathcal F^\bullet\subseteq\mathcal I^n\mathcal F^\bullet$, is a *Deligne system* for $j$. Its restriction to $U$ is a constant system in $D_{\mathrm{Coh}}^b(\mathcal O_U)$ with value $K=\mathcal F^\bullet|_U$. A *pro-isomorphism* refers to isomorphism in $\operatorname{Pro}(D_{\mathrm{Coh}}^b(\mathcal O_X))$, whose Hom sets into a constant object $L$ are $\operatorname*{colim}_n\operatorname{Hom}_{D_{\mathrm{Coh}}^b(X)}(K_n,L)$. Suppose $K\to L\to M\to K[1]$ is a distinguished triangle in $D_{\mathrm{Coh}}^b(\mathcal O_U)$. Then there exists an inverse system of distinguished triangles $K_n\to L_n\to M_n\to K_n[1]$ in $D_{\mathrm{Coh}}^b(\mathcal O_X)$ such that each of the three inverse systems is a Deligne system and the restriction of every displayed triangle to $U$ is isomorphic to the original triangle. This is a *systemwise existence* statement for representing exact triangles, not strict exactness of a naive functor to an abelian category.

conclusions: Colimits, tensors and (with finite-locally-free source) internal Homs are computed compatibly across the three big sites.

records.statement: Let $S$ be a scheme. For $\tau\in\{\mathrm{Zariski},\mathrm{\acute etale},\mathrm{fppf}\}$ consider the big ringed site $(\operatorname{Sch}/S)_\tau$ and its associated category of $\mathcal O$-modules; identify a quasi-coherent module on each site by the common pullback-section rule $\mathcal F^a(T)=\Gamma(T,f^*\mathcal F_S)$ from a quasi-coherent $\mathcal O_S$-module. (1) The category $\operatorname{QCoh}((\operatorname{Sch}/S)_{\mathrm{fppf}},\mathcal O)$ has all colimits; their images under each of the three associated-site inclusions agree with the ambient module-category colimits. records.title: Lemma — Power works

conclusions: $X_{\text{ft-pts}} \subset |X|$ is the set of closed points.
hypotheses: Let $S$ be a scheme and $X$ an algebraic space over $S$. Write $|X|$ for its underlying topological space, obtained from the equivalence classes of morphisms $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ from spectra of fields. The fibre product of algebraic spaces is understood in the category of algebraic spaces. For an étale presentation $U\to X$ by a scheme, $R=U\times_XU$ is its groupoid of arrows with projections $s,t:R\rightrightarrows U$. A morphism is representable if every base change along a map from a scheme has scheme source.

An algebraic space $X$ is decent if every point $x\in|X|$ admits a quasi-compact representing monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)\to X$. It is reasonable if every affine étale morphism $U\to X$ has universally bounded finite fibres, and very reasonable if it is Zariski-locally covered by quasi-compact surjective étale schemes. A morphism $f:X\to Y$ is *decent* (respectively reasonable, very reasonable or with property $(\beta)$) if $X\times_YT$ has that property for every scheme $T\to Y$. Property $(\beta)$ for a space means that every point can be represented by a monomorphism from a field spectrum.

For decent $X$ and $x\in|X|$, $\kappa(x)$ is the field associated with the representing monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)\to X$. An *elementary étale neighborhood* $(U,u)\to(X,x)$ is an étale scheme chart whose pointed field map $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(u)\to X$ is such a monomorphism. Its henselian local ring is $\mathcal O_{X,x}^{h}=\varinjlim_{(U,u)}\Gamma(U,\mathcal O_U)$ over the cofiltered category of elementary étale neighborhoods, and it agrees with $\mathcal O_{U,u}^h$ for any one of them. A decent space's point-set $|X|$ is sober and admits a dense open schematic locus when it has finitely many irreducible components.

An algebraic space $X$ is *Jacobson* if it admits an étale surjective cover by Jacobson schemes. A topological space $|X|$ is Jacobson if closed points are dense in every closed subset. A *finite type point* $x\in X_{\mathrm{ft\text{-}pts}}$ is a point represented by a morphism from a field spectrum locally of finite type over $X$. A decent locally Noetherian algebraic space has a sober underlying topological space, and its specialization relations agree locally with those on elementary étale scheme charts.

conclusions: The twisted right adjoint agrees with derived exact-support Hom on bounded-below inputs.
hypotheses: X qcqs, i pseudo-coherent closed immersion, K in D_QCoh^+.
records.statement:
Let $i:Z\hookrightarrow X$ be a closed immersion of schemes with ideal sheaf $\mathcal I\subseteq\mathcal O_X$. Write $R\mathcal Hom_Z(\mathcal O_Z,K)\in D(\mathcal O_Z)$ for the *exact-support right adjoint* to $Ri_*:D(\mathcal O_Z)\to D(\mathcal O_X)$, characterized by $Ri_*R\mathcal Hom_Z(\mathcal O_Z,K)\simeq R\mathcal Hom_{\mathcal O_X}(i_*\mathcal O_Z,K)$; affine locally for $X=\operatorname{Spec}A,Z=\operatorname{Spec}B$ it corresponds to $R\operatorname{Hom}_A(B,-)$ with its natural $B$-module structure. Assume $X$ is quasi-compact and quasi-separated and $i:Z\hookrightarrow X$ is a pseudo-coherent closed immersion. Let $a_i:D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}(\mathcal O_X)\to D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}(\mathcal O_Z)$ be the right adjoint to $Ri_*$. Then for every $K\in D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}^{+}(\mathcal O_X)$ there is a functorial isomorphism
\[
a_i(K)\xrightarrow{\sim}R\mathcal Hom_Z(\mathcal O_Z,K).
\]
The isomorphism is explicitly restricted to bounded-below quasi-coherent-derived inputs; it does not assert equality for arbitrary unbounded inputs.

Write $|X|$ for its underlying topological space, obtained from the equivalence classes of morphisms $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ from spectra of fields. The fibre product of algebraic spaces is understood in the category of algebraic spaces. For an étale presentation $U\to X$ by a scheme, $R=U\times_XU$ is its groupoid of arrows with projections $s,t:R\rightrightarrows U$. A morphism is representable if every base change along a map from a scheme has scheme source.

For $x\in|X|$, condition $(\alpha)_x$ means every affine étale morphism $U\to X$ has only finitely many points over $x$. Condition $(\beta)_x$ means there is a monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ representing $x$. Condition $(\gamma)_x$ means there is a quasi-compact monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ representing $x$, equivalently for every affine étale $U\to X$ both fibres over $x$ of $|U|\to|X|$ and $|U\times_XU|\to|X|$ are finite. The conditions $(\alpha),(\beta),(\gamma)$ mean the corresponding pointwise property holds at every $x$.

An algebraic space $X$ is *decent* when it satisfies $(\gamma)$, equivalently every point $x$ can be represented by a quasi-compact monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)\to X$. It is *reasonable* when it satisfies $(\delta)$, equivalently the fibres of every affine étale presentation $U\to X$ are universally bounded. It is *very reasonable* when it satisfies $(\epsilon)$, equivalently it has a Zariski-local quasi-compact surjective étale cover by schemes. The implications scheme or quasi-separated $\Rightarrow$ very reasonable $\Rightarrow$ reasonable $\Rightarrow$ decent hold.

For $x\in|X|$ and an étale morphism $U\to X$, write $(U,u)\to(X,x)$ for a pointed étale neighborhood. It is *elementary* when $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(u)\to X$ is a monomorphism representing $x$. When $X$ is decent, such neighborhoods are cofiltered: they exist, any two have a common refinement and parallel arrows can be equalized after refinement. The residue field $\kappa(x)$ is the field of the unique representing monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)\to X$, and the henselian local ring $\mathcal O_{X,x}^{h}$ is the filtered colimit of $\Gamma(U,\mathcal O_U)$ over elementary étale neighborhoods; equivalently $\mathcal O_{X,x}^{h}\cong\mathcal O_{U,u}^{h}$ for any elementary étale neighborhood.

For points $a,b$ of a topological space, $b\leadsto a$ means $a\in\overline{\{b\}}$, i.e., $a$ is a specialization of $b$. The space is $T_0$ (Kolmogorov) when distinct points have distinct closures, and sober when every irreducible closed subset has exactly one generic point. A subset is locally constructible if its intersection with every quasi-compact open subset is a finite union of locally closed subsets. An algebraic space has a locally constructible subset in the étale sense when its inverse image in every étale scheme chart is locally constructible.

records.statement:
In a triangulated derived category D(A), a **compact object** K is one for which Hom(K,⊕_i M_i)≅⊕_iHom(K,M_i) for **arbitrary** families. A distinct bounded-below-only compactness property is used in D^+(O): it is tested only on direct sums M=⊕ M_i that are bounded below as a whole. For a site object U, j_{U!}O_U is extension by zero from the ringed slice, and its representability relates Hom to derived sections over U. A quasi-compact **site object** is understood in the site-covering sense, not necessarily a quasi-compact topological space.

Let $(\mathcal{C}, \mathcal{O})$ be a ringed site. Assume every object of
$\mathcal{C}$ has a covering by quasi-compact objects. Then every
compact object of $D(\mathcal{O})$ is a direct summand in $D(\mathcal{O})$
of a finite complex whose terms are finite direct sums of
$\mathcal{O}$-modules of the form $j_!\mathcal{O}_U$
where $U$ is a quasi-compact object of $\mathcal{C}$.

records.statement:
Let $S$ be a scheme. Let $f : X \to Z$, $g : Y \to Z$ and $Z \to T$
be morphisms of formal algebraic spaces over $S$. Consider the induced
morphism $i : X \times_Z Y \to X \times_T Y$. Then
\begin{enumerate}
\item $i$ is representable (by schemes), locally of finite type,
locally quasi-finite, separated, and a monomorphism,
\item if $Z \to T$ is separated, then $i$ is a closed immersion, and
\item if $Z \to T$ is quasi-separated, then $i$ is quasi-compact.
\end{enumerate}

\item The morphism $f$ is flat.

$\mathcal{O}_S(V) \to \mathcal{O}_X(U)$ is flat.
\item There exists an open covering $S = \bigcup_{j \in J} V_j$
and open coverings $f^{-1}(V_j) = \bigcup_{i \in I_j} U_i$ such
that each of the morphisms $U_i \to V_j$, $j\in J, i\in I_j$

any open subschemes $U \subset X$, $V \subset S$ with $f(U) \subset V$
the restriction $f|_U : U \to V$ is flat.
hypotheses: Let $f : X \to S$ be a morphism of schemes.
records.statement:
Let $f : X \to S$ be a morphism of schemes.
The following are equivalent
\begin{enumerate}
\item The morphism $f$ is flat.
\item For every affine opens $U \subset X$, $V \subset S$
with $f(U) \subset V$ the ring map
$\mathcal{O}_S(V) \to \mathcal{O}_X(U)$ is flat.
\item There exists an open covering $S = \bigcup_{j \in J} V_j$
and open coverings $f^{-1}(V_j) = \bigcup_{i \in I_j} U_i$ such
that each of the morphisms $U_i \to V_j$, $j\in J, i\in I_j$
is flat.
\item There exists an affine open covering $S = \bigcup_{j \in J} V_j$
and affine open coverings $f^{-1}(V_j) = \bigcup_{i \in I_j} U_i$ such
that $\mathcal{O}_S(V_j) \to \mathcal{O}_X(U_i)$ is flat, for all
$j\in J, i\in I_j$.
\end{enumerate}
Moreover, if $f$ is flat then for
any open subschemes $U \subset X$, $V \subset S$ with $f(U) \subset V$
the restriction $f|_U : U \to V$ is flat.

hypotheses: C is a site with a collection B of weakly contractible objects covering all its objects.
O is a sheaf of rings on C.
records.statement:
On a site C, an object U is **weakly contractible** if every epimorphism of sheaves of sets F→G induces a surjection on sections F(U)→G(U). This is stronger than topological weak contractibility of a space. For a ringed site (C,O), extension by zero j_{U!}O_U is the left adjoint to localization/restriction at U. Let B⊂Ob(C) consist of weakly contractible objects such that **every** site object admits a covering by members of B. The assertion is a seven-part conjunction, including exactness, truncation completeness, derived products and inverse-limit formulas. The tower/derived-limit results use **countable sequential** inverse systems, with R^1lim described by the difference map on products.

Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a site. Let $\mathcal{B} \subset \Ob(\mathcal{C})$
such that every $U \in \mathcal{B}$ is weakly contractible and
every object of $\mathcal{C}$ has a covering by elements of $\mathcal{B}$.
Let $\mathcal{O}$ be a sheaf of rings on $\mathcal{C}$. Then
\begin{enumerate}
\item A complex $\mathcal{F}_1 \to \mathcal{F}_2 \to \mathcal{F}_3$
of $\mathcal{O}$-modules is exact, if and only if
$\mathcal{F}_1(U) \to \mathcal{F}_2(U) \to \mathcal{F}_3(U)$
is exact for all $U \in \mathcal{B}$.
\item Every object $K$ of $D(\mathcal{O})$ is a derived limit
of its canonical truncations: $K = R\lim \tau_{\geq -n} K$.
\item Given an inverse system
$\ldots \to \mathcal{F}_3 \to \mathcal{F}_2 \to \mathcal{F}_1$
with surjective transition maps, the projection
$\lim \mathcal{F}_n \to \mathcal{F}_1$ is surjective.
\item Products are exact on $\textit{Mod}(\mathcal{O})$.
\item Products on $D(\mathcal{O})$ can be computed by taking
products of any representative complexes.
\item If $(\mathcal{F}_n)$ is an inverse system of $\mathcal{O}$-modules,
then $R^p\lim \mathcal{F}_n = 0$ for all $p > 1$ and
$$
R^1\lim \mathcal{F}_n  =
\Coker(\prod \mathcal{F}_n \to \prod \mathcal{F}_n)
$$
where the map is $(x_n) \mapsto (x_n - f(x_{n + 1}))$.
\item If $(K_n)$ is an inverse system of objects of $D(\mathcal{O})$,
then there are short exact sequences
$$
0 \to R^1\lim H^{p - 1}(K_n) \to H^p(R\lim K_n) \to
\lim H^p(K_n) \to 0
$$
\end{enumerate}

records.title: Lemma — When surjective local

conclusions: Canonical equivalence of global RHom complexes.
hypotheses: f qcqs; E,K quasi-coherent-derived; a_f right adjoint.
records.statement:
Let $D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}(\mathcal O_T)$ be the unbounded derived category of complexes of $\mathcal O_T$-modules having quasi-coherent cohomology sheaves. For a morphism $f:X\to Y$ of quasi-compact and quasi-separated schemes, denote by $a_f:D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}(\mathcal O_Y)\to D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}(\mathcal O_X)$ the right adjoint to the derived pushforward $Rf_*$. Thus $\operatorname{Hom}_X(E,a_f(K))\cong\operatorname{Hom}_Y(Rf_*E,K)$ naturally in $E,K$, with unit $\eta_f:\mathrm{id}\to a_f Rf_*$ and counit $\operatorname{Tr}_f:Rf_*a_f\to\mathrm{id}$. This right adjoint is not in general the Grothendieck upper-shriek functor $f^!$. For any $E\in D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}(\mathcal O_X)$ and $K\in D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}(\mathcal O_Y)$ the canonical morphism on global derived Hom complexes
\[
R\operatorname{Hom}_X(E,a_f(K))\longrightarrow R\operatorname{Hom}_Y(Rf_*E,K),
\]
induced by $Rf_*R\mathcal Hom_X(E,a_f(K))\to R\mathcal Hom_Y(Rf_*E,K)$ and derived global sections, is a quasi-isomorphism (hence an isomorphism in the derived category of abelian groups). This is stronger than merely the degree-zero Hom-set adjunction but does *not* imply that the underlying sheaf-level map is an isomorphism before quasi-coherating.

hypotheses: Fix a prime $p$ and a divided power scheme $(S,\mathcal I,\gamma)$ over $\mathbf Z_{(p)}$, where $\mathcal I$ is a quasi-coherent ideal with divided powers. Set $S_0=V(\mathcal I)$ and choose a morphism $X\to S_0$ on which $p$ is locally nilpotent. A divided power thickening of $X/S$ is a triple $(U,T,\delta)$ with a closed immersion $U\hookrightarrow T$ inducing a homeomorphism on topological spaces, divided powers $\delta$ on its ideal $\mathcal J_T$, a compatible morphism of divided power schemes $T\to S$, and a map $U\to X$. These objects with compatible maps form $\mathrm{CRIS}(X/S)$; its full subcategory $\mathrm{Cris}(X/S)$ has $U\to X$ an open immersion. Both carry the Zariski topology (covers arise from Zariski covers of $T$ compatible with $U$). The forgetful functor $\mathrm{CRIS}(X/S)\to\operatorname{Sch}/X$ sends $(U,T,\delta)$ to $U$.

Given a ring map $A\to B$ and a divided power ideal $(J,\delta)$ on $B$, a divided power $A$-derivation $d:B\to M$ into a $B$-module is additive, vanishes on $A$, satisfies $d(bb')=b\,d(b')+b'\,d(b)$, and $d(\delta_n(x))=\delta_{n-1}(x)d(x)$ for $x\in J$. The universal module representing such derivations is $\Omega_{B/A,\delta}$ with universal map $d_{B/A,\delta}$. The ordinary Kähler differential module $\Omega_{B/A}$ represents all $A$-derivations. For a divided power scheme $(T,\mathcal J,\delta)\to S$, the sheaf $\Omega_{T/S,\delta}$ represents divided power derivations and is the quotient of $\Omega_{T/S}$ by the divided-power derivative relations.

On the small crystalline site $\mathrm{Cris}(X/S)$, the crystalline structure sheaf $\mathcal O_{X/S}$ restricts to $\mathcal O_T$ on an object $(U,T,\delta)$. A sheaf $\mathcal F$ of $\mathcal O_{X/S}$-modules restricts to a sheaf $\mathcal F_T$ on $T$. It is a crystal if each pullback comparison map $f^*\mathcal F_T\to\mathcal F_{T'}$ for a morphism $(U',T',\delta')\to(U,T,\delta)$ is an isomorphism. It is locally quasi-coherent if every $\mathcal F_T$ is quasi-coherent, and quasi-coherent as a module on the site if it is locally presented by free $\mathcal O_{X/S}$-modules. The sheaf $\Omega_{X/S}$ is the universal divided power sheaf of differentials for the structure morphism of the crystalline site to the Zariski site of $S$; it restricts to $\Omega_{T/S,\delta}$ on each object.

records.title: Lemma — Base change finite presentation

conclusions: $c^*\omega_Y \cong \omega_X$.
hypotheses: Let $k$ be a field. A proper curve over $k$ is a proper integral $k$-scheme of Krull dimension one; a proper $k$-scheme of dimension one need not be integral. For any proper such scheme $X$ with $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X)=k$, define its genus as $g(X)=\dim_k H^1(X,\mathcal O_X)$. If $X$ is one-dimensional, Cohen–Macaulay and equidimensional, its coherent dualizing module is $\omega_X=H^{-1}(f^!k)$ for $f:X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$; it is invertible when $X$ is Gorenstein.

A closed point $x$ of a one-dimensional locally finite type $k$-scheme $X$ is a *node* if for an algebraic closure $\bar k$ some point $\bar x$ of $X_{\bar k}$ over $x$ has completed local ring $\bar k[[u,v]]/(uv)$. All singularities of $X$ are *at worst nodal* if each closed point is smooth over $k$ or a node. Equivalently at a node $\kappa(x)/k$ is separable and $\widehat{\mathcal O}_{X,x}\cong\kappa(x)[[u,v]]/(au^2+buv+cv^2)$ for a nondegenerate binary quadratic form (whose discriminant is nonzero, including in characteristic $2$). Such curves are Gorenstein and geometrically reduced.

For a proper Cohen–Macaulay $k$-scheme $X$ of dimension one with $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X)=k$, put $\omega_X=H^{-1}(f^!k)$, $g=\dim_kH^1(X,\mathcal O_X)$, and for invertible $\mathcal L$ let $\deg(\mathcal L)=\chi(X,\mathcal L)-\chi(X,\mathcal O_X)$. If $X$ is Gorenstein, $\omega_X$ is an invertible sheaf of degree $2g-2$. For a zero-dimensional subscheme $Z\subset X$, $\deg(Z)=\dim_kH^0(Z,\mathcal O_Z)$.

For a proper $k$-scheme $X$ of dimension one with $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X)=k$ and at-worst-nodal singularities, a *stable curve* (in the situation $g\ge2$) has no rational tails or rational bridges, equivalently each genus-zero irreducible component meets the remainder of $X$ in at least three geometric points. Its dualizing sheaf $\omega_X$ is invertible. A contraction to a stable curve means a proper morphism $c:X\to X_{\mathrm{st}}$ obtained by successively contracting rational tails and bridges and whose target has no such components.

For a proper $k$-scheme $X$ of dimension one with $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X)=k$ and at-worst-nodal singularities, a *rational tail* $C\subset X$ is an integral irreducible component such that $X'$ (the scheme-theoretic closure of $X\setminus C$) is nonempty, $C\cap X'$ is a single reduced point $x$, the map $H^0(C,\mathcal O_C)\to\kappa(x)$ is an isomorphism, and $g(C)=0$. The contraction of the tail is $c:X\to X'$ equal to the identity on $X'$ and collapsing $C$ to $x$ via $C\to\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)$. It satisfies $c_*\mathcal O_X=\mathcal O_{X'}$ and $R^1c_*\mathcal O_X=0$.

For a proper $k$-scheme $X$ of dimension one with $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X)=k$ and at-worst-nodal singularities, a *rational bridge* $C\subset X$ is an integral irreducible component such that $X'$ (the scheme-theoretic closure of $X\setminus C$) is nonempty, $C$ has genus zero, and the scheme-theoretic intersection $C\cap X'$ is finite of degree two over $k'=H^0(C,\mathcal O_C)$ (either two $k'$-points or a degree-two separable point). Its contraction $c:X\to Y$ collapses $C$ to a point $y$ and is obtained from the pushout $Y=X'\amalg_{C\cap X'}\operatorname{Spec}k'$. It satisfies $c_*\mathcal O_X=\mathcal O_Y$ and $R^1c_*\mathcal O_X=0$; $Y$ remains at worst nodal. The genus of $Y$ equals that of $X$.

Assume
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\mathcal{O}_Y = c_*\mathcal{O}_X$ and $R^1c_*\mathcal{O}_X = 0$,

conclusions:
Let $X$ be a connected scheme. Let $\Lambda$ be a ring and let
$\mathcal{F}$ be a locally constant sheaf of $\Lambda$-modules.
Then there exists a $\Lambda$-module $M$ and an \'etale covering
$\{U_i \to X\}$ such that $\mathcal{F}|_{U_i} \cong \underline{M}|_{U_i}$.
The claim is interpreted using the preceding explicit definitions; retain exactly the original assumptions and conclusion on the small étale site (distinguishing finite from finite-type local fibres).
hypotheses: On the **small étale site** $X_{\acute et}$ of a scheme $X$, a *constant sheaf* $\underline E$ is the sheafification of the constant presheaf with value a set $E$ (similarly an abelian group or $\Lambda$-module). A sheaf $\mathcal F$ is *locally constant* if there is an étale cover $\{U_i\to X\}$ on which it becomes isomorphic to a constant sheaf; it is *finite locally constant* for set-valued sheaves if its constant fibre sets are finite, and *finite type locally constant* for $\Lambda$-modules if its local fibre modules are finitely generated. For an étale map $U\to X$, its representable sheaf is $h_U(V)=\operatorname{Hom}_X(V,U)$. In an abelian category a *weak Serre subcategory* is closed under kernels, cokernels and extensions (without necessarily all subobjects).

Let $A$ be a ring, $(I, \leq)$ a directed set and $(B_i, \varphi_{ij})$ a
system of $A$-algebras. Set $B = \colim_{i\in I} B_i$. Let $X \to \Spec(A)$
be a quasi-compact and quasi-separated morphism of schemes. Let
$\mathcal{F}$ an abelian sheaf on $X_\etale$.
Denote $Y_i = X \times_{\Spec(A)} \Spec(B_i)$,
$Y = X \times_{\Spec(A)} \Spec(B)$,
$\mathcal{G}_i = (Y_i \to X)^{-1}\mathcal{F}$ and
$\mathcal{G} = (Y \to X)^{-1}\mathcal{F}$. Then
$$
H_\etale^p(Y, \mathcal{G}) =
\colim_{i\in I} H_\etale^p (Y_i, \mathcal{G}_i).
$$

conclusions:
Let $S$ be a scheme. The \'etale topos of $S$ is independent
(up to canonical equivalence) of the construction of the small
\'etale site in Definition \ref{definition-tau-site}.
This is a **canonical equivalence of small étale categories of sheaves of sets** for different partial universe choices, by their common affine étale site. It does **not** assert independence for arbitrary big τ-topoi.
hypotheses:
Fix a scheme $S$. The **big $\tau$-site** $(\mathrm{Sch}/S)_\tau$ is a small-universe-selected category of $S$-schemes with covering families of type $\tau\in\{\mathrm{fppf},\mathrm{syntomic},\mathrm{smooth},\mathrm{\acute etale},\mathrm{Zariski}\}$. The **small étale site** $S_{\acute etale}$ has as objects étale $S$-schemes and as covers jointly surjective étale families; the **small Zariski site** $S_{\mathrm{Zar}}$ has open subschemes as objects. These are different sites; restriction from a big to a small site is not an identity of categories. For an abelian sheaf $\mathcal F$ on a site, $H^p_\tau(U,\mathcal F)$ denotes the $p$-th right derived functor of its sections over the site object $U$. A *standard $\tau$-cover of an affine $U$* is a **finite** jointly surjective family of affine maps $U_i\to U$, each flat finitely presented for fppf, standard syntomic, standard smooth, étale, or standard principal-open immersion, respectively.

A *partial universe* is a sufficiently large set of schemes and morphisms used to choose a **small** big-$\tau$ site, closed under relevant finite limits and with every external $\tau$-cover of an object admitting a refinement internally; distinct choices give inclusions of corresponding sites. A small étale *topos* of $S$ is $\operatorname{Sh}(S_{\acute etale})$, the category of set-valued sheaves; it is not the category of all big-site sheaves.

conclusions: j_{U!}O_U is compact in D(O).

records.statement:
In a triangulated derived category D(A), a **compact object** K is one for which Hom(K,⊕_i M_i)≅⊕_iHom(K,M_i) for **arbitrary** families. A distinct bounded-below-only compactness property is used in D^+(O): it is tested only on direct sums M=⊕ M_i that are bounded below as a whole. For a site object U, j_{U!}O_U is extension by zero from the ringed slice, and its representability relates Hom to derived sections over U. Being both **quasi-compact** (in the site sense) and **weakly contractible** is required for a site object U; neither property alone is the stated hypothesis.

Let $(\mathcal{C}, \mathcal{O})$ be a ringed site. Let $U$
be an object of $\mathcal{C}$ which is quasi-compact and
weakly contractible. Then
$j_!\mathcal{O}_U$ is a compact object of $D(\mathcal{O})$.

records.title: Lemma — Extend

conclusions:
Let $(R, \mathfrak m, \kappa)$ be a local ring and
$\kappa\subset\kappa^{sep}$ a separable algebraic closure.
There exist canonical flat local ring maps $R \to R^h \to R^{sh}$ where
\begin{enumerate}
\item $R^h$, $R^{sh}$ are filtered colimits of \'etale $R$-algebras,
\item $R^h$ is henselian, $R^{sh}$ is strictly henselian,
\item $\mathfrak m R^h$ (resp.\ $\mathfrak m R^{sh}$) is the
maximal ideal of $R^h$ (resp.\ $R^{sh}$), and
\item $\kappa = R^h/\mathfrak m R^h$, and
$\kappa^{sep} = R^{sh}/\mathfrak m R^{sh}$ as extensions of $\kappa$.
\end{enumerate}
The maps R→R^h→R^sh are **flat and local**, both rings are *filtered colimits of étale R-algebras*, and the residue-field extensions are respectively κ and the **chosen κ^sep**. The strict construction depends on a separable-closure choice; 'canonical' means relative to that choice.

The *small étale topos* is $\operatorname{Sh}(S_{\acute etale})$ (sheaves of sets), and $\operatorname{Ab}(S_{\acute etale})$ consists of abelian sheaves. The **big $\tau$-site** $(\mathrm{Sch}/S)_\tau$ for $\tau\in\{\mathrm{Zariski},\acute etale,\mathrm{smooth},\mathrm{syntomic},\mathrm{fppf}\}$ has all suitable universe-selected $S$-schemes as objects, not only étale ones. A site/topos has *enough points* when a family of its point-stalk functors detects isomorphisms of sheaves. This property is **not** a classification of all points.

A **henselian local ring** $(R,\mathfrak m,\kappa)$ is a local ring satisfying Hensel's lifting criterion: for each **monic** $f\in R[T]$ and each simple root $\bar a\in\kappa$ of $\bar f$, there is a root $a\in R$ reducing to $\bar a$. A local ring is **strictly henselian** if henselian with separably closed residue field. A finite $R$-algebra is a ring $A$ finite as an $R$-module. The *henselization* $R^h$ is a flat local ind-étale $R$-algebra henselian with residue field $\kappa$; given a **chosen separable closure** $\kappa^{sep}$, the *strict henselization* $R^{sh}$ is a flat local ind-étale algebra with separably closed residue field $\kappa^{sep}$.

hypotheses: Let $S$ be a locally Noetherian universally catenary scheme equipped with a dimension function $\delta:S\to\mathbf Z$. A $q$-cycle on $T$ is a locally finite integral linear combination of integral closed subschemes of $\delta$-dimension $q$; $Z_q(T)$ is the group of these cycles. For a closed subscheme $W$ of dimension at most $q$, $[W]_q$ is the sum of the $q$-dimensional components weighted by generic-point length multiplicities. The Chow group $\mathrm{CH}_q(T)$ is $Z_q(T)$ modulo rational equivalence generated by locally finite principal divisors on integral closed subschemes of dimension $q+1$.

For a flat morphism $h:T'\to T$ of relative dimension $r$, the flat pullback $h^*:Z_q(T)\to Z_{q+r}(T')$ sends $[W]$ to the cycle $[T'\times_TW]_{q+r}$ weighted by the lengths at generic points of components. It descends to Chow groups.

$\mathrm{CH}_k(X)=Z_k(X)/\!\sim_{\mathrm{rat}}$, where rational equivalence is generated by locally finite sums of principal divisors of nonzero rational functions on integral closed subschemes of dimension $k+1$, pushed into $X$. Then either $f(X)$ is contained in a proper closed subscheme
of $Y$, or $f$ is dominant and the extension of function fields

records.title: Lemma — Permanence quasi finite

conclusions: $L_{B/A}$ is quasi-isomorphic to $I/I^2[1]$.
hypotheses: For a ring map $A\to B$, let $\Omega_{B/A}$ be the module of Kähler differentials. The cotangent complex $L_{B/A}\in D(B)$ is obtained from the standard augmented simplicial polynomial $A$-algebra resolution $P_\bullet\to B$, where $P_0=A[B]$, $P_1=A[A[B]]$, etc., by taking the chain complex (in nonpositive cohomological degrees) associated to the simplicial $B$-module $\Omega_{P_\bullet/A}\otimes_{P_\bullet}B$. Here $A[E]$ denotes the polynomial algebra freely generated by a set $E$, $D(B)$ is the derived category of $B$-modules, and $H^i$ denotes degree-$i$ cohomology.

A quasi-isomorphism is a map of complexes inducing an isomorphism on every cohomology module. We write $M[0]$ for a module concentrated in degree zero, $M[1]$ for a module in degree $-1$, $\otimes_A^{\mathbf L}$ for derived tensor product, and $\tau_{\geq -1}$ for the standard truncation in cohomological degrees at least $-1$. The module $\Omega_{B/A}$ is generated by symbols $db$ subject to additivity, the Leibniz rule, and $da=0$ for $a\in A$.

An ordered sequence $(f_1,\dots,f_r)$ in a ring $A$ is Koszul-regular if the Koszul complex $K(f_1,\dots,f_r;A)$ has no positive-degree homology. A Koszul ideal is locally generated by a Koszul-regular sequence. A local complete intersection (lci) ring map $A\to B$ locally factors as a smooth algebra map followed by a quotient whose kernel is generated by a regular sequence. A perfect complex is locally quasi-isomorphic to a bounded complex of finite projective modules; Tor-amplitude in $[-1,0]$ means its derived tensor product with any module has cohomology only in degrees $-1,0$.

records.title: Lemma — Countable fg tensor

conclusions: The canonical mate Rg'_*a'→a Rg_* is an isomorphism.
hypotheses: Cartesian qcqs square, g flat or f and g Tor independent, and right adjoints as defined.
records.statement:
Let $D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}(\mathcal O_T)$ be the unbounded derived category of complexes of $\mathcal O_T$-modules having quasi-coherent cohomology sheaves. For a morphism $f:X\to Y$ of quasi-compact and quasi-separated schemes, denote by $a_f:D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}(\mathcal O_Y)\to D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}(\mathcal O_X)$ the right adjoint to the derived pushforward $Rf_*$. Thus $\operatorname{Hom}_X(E,a_f(K))\cong\operatorname{Hom}_Y(Rf_*E,K)$ naturally in $E,K$, with unit $\eta_f:\mathrm{id}\to a_f Rf_*$ and counit $\operatorname{Tr}_f:Rf_*a_f\to\mathrm{id}$. This right adjoint is not in general the Grothendieck upper-shriek functor $f^!$. Consider a cartesian square of quasi-compact quasi-separated schemes
\[
\begin{matrix}
X'&\xrightarrow{g'}&X\\
f'\downarrow&&\downarrow f\\
Y'&\xrightarrow{g}&Y
\end{matrix}
\]
where $f$ and $g$ are *Tor-independent*, meaning the higher Tor sheaves of $\mathcal O_X$ and $\mathcal O_{Y'}$ over $\mathcal O_Y$ vanish. Write $a=a_f$ and $a'=a_{f'}$ for the respective right adjoints of derived pushforward. The usual derived base-change map is $\beta:Lg^*Rf_*\to Rf'_*L(g')^*$; under Tor-independence it is an isomorphism. Its adjoint mate is the isomorphism $\xi:Rg'_*a'\xrightarrow{\sim} a Rg_*$. The duality base-change map is the natural transformation $\alpha:L(g')^*a\to a' Lg^*$ obtained by composing unit $\mathrm{id}\to Rg_*Lg^*$, $\xi^{-1}$, and counit $L(g')^*Rg'_*\to\mathrm{id}$. Then the canonical adjoint-mate transformation $\xi:Rg'_*a'\to a\,Rg_*$, considered as a natural transformation from $D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}(\mathcal O_{Y'})$ to $D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}(\mathcal O_X)$, is an isomorphism. This holds if $g$ is flat, and more generally whenever $f$ and $g$ are Tor-independent; the square need not be proper.

\item The morphism $f$ is unramified (resp.\ G-unramified) at $x$.
\item The fibre $X_s$ is unramified over $\kappa(s)$ at $x$.
\item The $\mathcal{O}_{X, x}$-module $\Omega_{X/S, x}$ is zero.
\item The $\mathcal{O}_{X_s, x}$-module $\Omega_{X_s/s, x}$ is zero.

\Omega_{X_s/s, x} \otimes_{\mathcal{O}_{X_s, x}} \kappa(x) =
\Omega_{X/S, x} \otimes_{\mathcal{O}_{X, x}} \kappa(x)
$$
is zero.
\item We have $\mathfrak m_s\mathcal{O}_{X, x} = \mathfrak m_x$
and the field extension $\kappa(x)/\kappa(s)$ is finite
separable.
\end{enumerate}

hypotheses: Let $S$ be a locally Noetherian universally catenary scheme equipped with a dimension function $\delta:S\to\mathbf Z$. For any $S$-scheme $T$ locally of finite type, write $\delta_T(t)=\delta(f(t))+\operatorname{trdeg}_{\kappa(f(t))}\kappa(t)$; for integral closed $W\subset T$, let $\dim_\delta W=\delta_T(\eta_W)$.

A $q$-cycle on $T$ is a locally finite integral linear combination of integral closed subschemes of $\delta$-dimension $q$; $Z_q(T)$ is the group of these cycles. For a closed subscheme $W$ of dimension at most $q$, $[W]_q$ is the sum of the $q$-dimensional components weighted by generic-point length multiplicities. The Chow group $\mathrm{CH}_q(T)$ is $Z_q(T)$ modulo rational equivalence generated by locally finite principal divisors on integral closed subschemes of dimension $q+1$.

For a morphism $f:X\to Y$ and integer $p$, a bivariant class $c\in A^p(X\to Y)$ is a collection of homomorphisms $c_T:\mathrm{CH}_q(T)\to\mathrm{CH}_{q-p}(X\times_YT)$ indexed by $T\to Y$ and $q$, satisfying: (i) for proper $h:T'\to T$, $c_T(h_*\beta)=h_{X,*}c_{T'}(\beta)$; (ii) for flat $h$ of fixed relative dimension, $c_{T'}(h^*\alpha)=h_X^*c_T(\alpha)$; (iii) for $i:E\hookrightarrow T$ the zero scheme of a section of an invertible sheaf, $c_E(i^*\alpha)=i_X^*c_T(\alpha)$, with $h_X,i_X$ the base changes. Composition of families gives products $A^p(X\to Y)\times A^q(Y\to Z)\to A^{p+q}(X\to Z)$, and $A^*(X)=\bigoplus_pA^p(X\to X)$.

For a finite locally free sheaf $\mathcal E$ of rank $r$ on $X$, its operational Chern classes are $c_j(\mathcal E)\in A^j(X)$, with $c_0=1$, $c_j=0$ for $j>r$, and total class $c(\mathcal E)=\sum_jc_j(\mathcal E)$. For an integral closed $W\subset X$ of $\delta$-dimension $n$, the classes $c_j(\mathcal E|_W)\cap[W]$ in $\mathrm{CH}_{n-j}(W)$ are characterized via the projective bundle $\pi:\mathbf P(\mathcal E|_W)\to W$ with tautological quotient $\mathcal O(1)$ by $\sum_{i=0}^r(-1)^i c_1(\mathcal O(1))^i\cap\pi^*c_{r-i}=0$ with $c_0=[W]$. Extend to general cycles by sum and proper pushforward, then to Chow groups.

For a locally free $\mathcal E$ with formal Chern roots $x_1,\ldots,x_r$ (elementary symmetric polynomials equal to $c_i(\mathcal E)$), put $P_p(\mathcal E)=\sum_{j=1}^r x_j^p$, where $P_0=r$, and $\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal E)=\sum_{p\geq0}P_p(\mathcal E)/p!$. Each $P_p$ is the universal Newton polynomial in the Chern classes, and the degree-$p$ Chern character lies in $A^p(X)\otimes\mathbf Q$.

The dual $\mathcal E^\vee=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O_X}(\mathcal E,\mathcal O_X)$.

then we have $c_i(\psi^2(\alpha)) = 2^i c_i(\alpha)$ and
$ch_i(\psi^2(\alpha)) = 2^i ch_i(\alpha)$

$F' : D^b_{\textit{Coh}}(\mathcal{O}_X) \to D^b_{\textit{Coh}}(\mathcal{O}_Y)$

records.title: Lemma — Exact functor preserving Coh

conclusions: f^!O_Y is a single coherent target-flat module shifted by the relative dimension.
hypotheses: f CM in FTS_S, locally constant relative dimension d.
records.statement: Fix a Noetherian base $S$. Write $\mathrm{FTS}_S$ for separated schemes of finite type over $S$, with $S$-morphisms. For $f:X\to Y$ in $\mathrm{FTS}_S$, choose a factorization $f=\bar f\circ j$ with $j:X\hookrightarrow\bar X$ an open immersion and $\bar f:\bar X\to Y$ proper. If $a_{\bar f}$ is the right adjoint to $R\bar f_*$ on unbounded quasi-coherent derived categories, define $f^!:D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}^+(\mathcal O_Y)\to D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}^+(\mathcal O_X)$ as $j^*a_{\bar f}$, independently (up to canonical identifications) of the chosen compactification. Suppose $f$ is a Cohen–Macaulay morphism: flat and locally of finite presentation with Cohen–Macaulay scheme-theoretic fibres. Let $d:X\to\mathbf Z_{\ge0}$ denote its locally constant relative fibre dimension. Then there is a coherent $\mathcal O_X$-module $\omega_{X/Y}$, flat over $Y$, for which $f^!\mathcal O_Y\simeq\omega_{X/Y}[d]$ locally on each component where $d$ is constant. Equivalently, the only nonzero cohomology sheaf occurs in cohomological degree $-d$ and is $\omega_{X/Y}$. The relative shift is componentwise when the relative dimension varies.

records.statement:
For functions $f_1,\ldots,f_r$ on a ringed space, regular means successive multiplication maps on $\mathcal O/(f_1,\ldots,f_{i-1})$ are injective; no nonzero-final-quotient condition is imposed here. Koszul-regular means the Koszul complex has zero homology in every positive degree; $H_1$-regular means its degree-one homology vanishes; quasi-regular means, with $\mathcal J=(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$ the ideal sheaf generated by the sequence, that $(\mathcal O/\mathcal J)[T_1,\ldots,T_r]\to\bigoplus_{n\geq0}\mathcal J^n/\mathcal J^{n+1}$ is an isomorphism, sending $T_i$ to $f_i$ modulo $\mathcal J^2$. An ideal sheaf is of a given type if near each point of $\operatorname{Supp}(\mathcal O/\mathcal J)$ it admits generators of that type. For a ring regular sequence one additionally requires the final quotient nonzero. An immersion is of a given type when its defining ideal on an open where it is closed is of that type. Relative quasi/$H_1$-regular means also that its source is flat over the base. Let
$$
\xymatrix{
Y \ar[rd] \ar[rr]_i & & X \ar[ld] \\
& S
}
$$
be a commutative diagram of morphisms of schemes.
Assume that $Y \to S$ is syntomic, $X \to S$ smooth, and
$i$ an immersion. Then $i$ is a regular immersion.

A homomorphism of divided power rings carries distinguished ideals into one another and commutes with all divided power operations.

For a divided power ring $(A,I,\gamma)$, an $A$-algebra $B$ and an ideal $J\subset B$ containing $IB$, the divided power envelope $D_{B,\gamma}(J)=(D,\bar J,\bar\gamma)$ is the universal divided power $(A,I,\gamma)$-algebra equipped with a ring map $B\to D$ carrying $J$ into $\bar J$: maps $D\to(C,K,\delta)$ of divided power $A$-algebras correspond naturally to $A$-algebra maps $B\to C$ carrying $J$ into $K$. Given a ring map $A\to B$ and a divided power ideal $(J,\delta)$ on $B$, a divided power $A$-derivation $d:B\to M$ into a $B$-module is additive, vanishes on $A$, satisfies $d(bb')=b\,d(b')+b'\,d(b)$, and $d(\delta_n(x))=\delta_{n-1}(x)d(x)$ for $x\in J$. A $2$-periodic complex $(M,N,\varphi,\psi)$ over $R$ consists of maps $\varphi:M\to N$ and $\psi:N\to M$ with $\psi\varphi=0=\varphi\psi$. Its two cohomology modules are $H^0=\ker\varphi/\operatorname{im}\psi$ and $H^1=\ker\psi/\operatorname{im}\varphi$. When both have finite length, $e_R(M,N,\varphi,\psi)=\operatorname{length}_R H^0-\operatorname{length}_R H^1$. A $(2,1)$-periodic complex $(M,\varphi,\psi)$ is the special case $M=N$.

Let $R$ be a ring. Let $M$ be an $R$-module.

such that $\varphi^n = 0$ and such that $\Ker(\varphi)/\Im(\varphi^{n - 1})$
has finite length as an $R$-module.
Then
$$
e_R(M, \varphi^i, \varphi^{n - i}) = 0
$$
for $i = 0, \ldots, n$.

records.title: Lemma — When shriek

conclusions:
$x$ is a closed point of $|X|$ if and only if
the morphism $Z_x \to X$ is a closed immersion.
hypotheses: Let $S$ be a scheme and $X$ an algebraic space over $S$. Write $|X|$ for its underlying topological space, obtained from the equivalence classes of morphisms $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ from spectra of fields. The fibre product of algebraic spaces is understood in the category of algebraic spaces. For an étale presentation $U\to X$ by a scheme, $R=U\times_XU$ is its groupoid of arrows with projections $s,t:R\rightrightarrows U$. A morphism is representable if every base change along a map from a scheme has scheme source.

For $x\in|X|$, condition $(\alpha)_x$ means every affine étale morphism $U\to X$ has only finitely many points over $x$. Condition $(\beta)_x$ means there is a monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ representing $x$. Condition $(\gamma)_x$ means there is a quasi-compact monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ representing $x$, equivalently for every affine étale $U\to X$ both fibres over $x$ of $|U|\to|X|$ and $|U\times_XU|\to|X|$ are finite. The conditions $(\alpha),(\beta),(\gamma)$ mean the corresponding pointwise property holds at every $x$.

An algebraic space $X$ is *decent* when it satisfies $(\gamma)$, equivalently every point $x$ can be represented by a quasi-compact monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)\to X$. It is *reasonable* when it satisfies $(\delta)$, equivalently the fibres of every affine étale presentation $U\to X$ are universally bounded. It is *very reasonable* when it satisfies $(\epsilon)$, equivalently it has a Zariski-local quasi-compact surjective étale cover by schemes. The implications scheme or quasi-separated $\Rightarrow$ very reasonable $\Rightarrow$ reasonable $\Rightarrow$ decent hold.

A *residual space* $Z_x\to X$ at $x\in|X|$ is the unique monomorphism from a reduced locally Noetherian algebraic space with singleton underlying topology whose image is $x$ and which is universal among morphisms of such spaces into $X$ representing $x$. A space is *locally separated* if its diagonal is an immersion; it is quasi-separated if its diagonal is quasi-compact and quasi-separated. A locally Noetherian algebraic space is one with an étale cover by locally Noetherian schemes.

Condition $(\beta)_x$ means there is a monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ representing $x$. Condition $(\gamma)_x$ means there is a quasi-compact monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ representing $x$, equivalently for every affine étale $U\to X$ both fibres over $x$ of $|U|\to|X|$ and $|U\times_XU|\to|X|$ are finite. The conditions $(\alpha),(\beta),(\gamma)$ mean the corresponding pointwise property holds at every $x$.

An algebraic space $X$ is *decent* when it satisfies $(\gamma)$, equivalently every point $x$ can be represented by a quasi-compact monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)\to X$. It is *reasonable* when it satisfies $(\delta)$, equivalently the fibres of every affine étale presentation $U\to X$ are universally bounded. It is *very reasonable* when it satisfies $(\epsilon)$, equivalently it has a Zariski-local quasi-compact surjective étale cover by schemes. The implications scheme or quasi-separated $\Rightarrow$ very reasonable $\Rightarrow$ reasonable $\Rightarrow$ decent hold.

A *residual space* $Z_x\to X$ at $x\in|X|$ is the unique monomorphism from a reduced locally Noetherian algebraic space with singleton underlying topology whose image is $x$ and which is universal among morphisms of such spaces into $X$ representing $x$. A space is *locally separated* if its diagonal is an immersion; it is quasi-separated if its diagonal is quasi-compact and quasi-separated. A locally Noetherian algebraic space is one with an étale cover by locally Noetherian schemes.

Let $S$ be a scheme. Let $X$ be an algebraic space over $S$. Let $x \in |X|$
with residual space $Z_x \subset X$. Assume $X$ is locally Noetherian.
Then $x$ is a closed point of $|X|$ if and only if
the morphism $Z_x \to X$ is a closed immersion.

records.title: Lemma — Product representable by spaces

conclusions: Derived local cohomology and derived completion are quasi-inverse between torsion and complete subcategories.
hypotheses: A arbitrary, I finitely generated, derived torsion and completion via augmented Čech.
records.statement:
Let $A$ be a commutative ring, $I=(f_1,\ldots,f_r)\subseteq A$ finitely generated, and $Z=V(I)\subseteq\operatorname{Spec}A$. Let $D_{\mathcal T_I}(A)\subseteq D(A)$ be the full triangulated subcategory of complexes whose cohomology modules are $I$-power torsion. Let $C_A(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$ be the *augmented alternating Čech complex* $[A\to\bigoplus_i A_{f_i}\to\bigoplus_{i<j}A_{f_if_j}\to\cdots\to A_{f_1\cdots f_r}]$, with $A$ in degree $0$, the standard alternating restriction differentials, and all terms flat. Define $R\Gamma_Z(K)=C_A(f_1,\ldots,f_r)\otimes_A^{\mathbf L}K\in D_{\mathcal T_I}(A)$, the right adjoint to the inclusion $D_{\mathcal T_I}(A)\hookrightarrow D(A)$. This is local cohomology, unlike $R\Gamma_I$ above for general non-Noetherian $A$. Define the *derived $I$-adic completion* of $K\in D(A)$ by $K^\wedge=R\operatorname{Hom}_A(C_A(f_1,\ldots,f_r),K)$, with its natural unit $K\to K^\wedge$. Let $D_{\rm comp}(A,I)$ be the full subcategory of derived $I$-complete complexes, i.e. those for which this unit is an isomorphism (equivalently $R\operatorname{Hom}_A(A_{f_i},K)=0$ for all $i$). These definitions use the derived Čech model and do not assume $A$ Noetherian or identify derived completion automatically with the naive inverse limit for arbitrary $K$. Then the restrictions
\[
R\Gamma_Z:D_{\rm comp}(A,I)\longrightarrow D_{\mathcal T_I}(A)
\quad\text{and}\quad
(-)^\wedge:D_{\mathcal T_I}(A)\longrightarrow D_{\rm comp}(A,I)
\]
are quasi-inverse exact equivalences of triangulated categories. More precisely $R\Gamma_Z(K^\wedge)\simeq R\Gamma_Z(K)$ and $(R\Gamma_ZK)^\wedge\simeq K^\wedge$ for any $K\in D(A)$. This is the derived torsion-completion equivalence, not classical equality of torsion and complete modules.

records.statement:

is finite (i.e. for each $n$ there exist indices $a_n,b_n$ such that $F^{a_n}K^n=K^n$ and $F^{b_n}K^n=0$). Then

\item the spectral sequence associated to $(K^\bullet, F)$ is bounded,
\item the filtration on each $H^n(K^\bullet)$ is finite,

to $H^*(K^\bullet)$,

and for some $r$ we have $E_r^{p, q} \in \mathcal{C}$ for all
$p, q \in \mathbf{Z}$, then $H^n(K^\bullet)$ is in $\mathcal{C}$.

records.title: Lemma — Genus normalization

conclusions: Relative perfectness and derived self-duality of the upper-shriek structure complex.
hypotheses: f flat in FTS_S.
records.statement:
Fix a Noetherian base scheme $S$ and let $\mathrm{FTS}_S$ be the category of schemes $T$ with separated finite-type structure map $T\to S$, with $S$-morphisms. For $f:X\to Y$ in this category, choose a *compactification* $X\xrightarrow{j}\overline X\xrightarrow{\bar f}Y$, with $j$ an open immersion and $\bar f$ proper. Since $\overline X,Y$ are qcqs, the derived pushforward $R\bar f_*:D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}(\mathcal O_{\bar X})\to D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}(\mathcal O_Y)$ has a right adjoint $a_{\bar f}$. Define the *upper-shriek* functor $f^!:D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}^+(\mathcal O_Y)\to D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}^+(\mathcal O_X)$ by $f^!(K)=j^*a_{\bar f}(K)$, with the canonical identifications between compactifications. This is different in general from the unrestricted right adjoint of $Rf_*$. Suppose $f:X\to Y$ in $\mathrm{FTS}_S$ is flat. An object $P\in D(\mathcal O_X)$ is *$Y$-perfect* if it is pseudo-coherent and has locally bounded Tor-amplitude relative to $f^{-1}\mathcal O_Y$. Then $f^!\mathcal O_Y$ is $Y$-perfect and the homothety map
\[
\mathcal O_X\xrightarrow{\sim}R\mathcal Hom_{\mathcal O_X}(f^!\mathcal O_Y,f^!\mathcal O_Y)
\]
is an isomorphism. Flatness here is part of a finite-type morphism in $\mathrm{FTS}_S$.

Write $|X|$ for its underlying topological space, obtained from the equivalence classes of morphisms $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ from spectra of fields. The fibre product of algebraic spaces is understood in the category of algebraic spaces. For an étale presentation $U\to X$ by a scheme, $R=U\times_XU$ is its groupoid of arrows with projections $s,t:R\rightrightarrows U$. A morphism is representable if every base change along a map from a scheme has scheme source.

An algebraic space $X$ is decent if every point $x\in|X|$ admits a quasi-compact representing monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)\to X$. It is reasonable if every affine étale morphism $U\to X$ has universally bounded finite fibres, and very reasonable if it is Zariski-locally covered by quasi-compact surjective étale schemes. A morphism $f:X\to Y$ is *decent* (respectively reasonable, very reasonable or with property $(\beta)$) if $X\times_YT$ has that property for every scheme $T\to Y$. Property $(\beta)$ for a space means that every point can be represented by a monomorphism from a field spectrum.

For decent $X$ and $x\in|X|$, $\kappa(x)$ is the field associated with the representing monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)\to X$. An *elementary étale neighborhood* $(U,u)\to(X,x)$ is an étale scheme chart whose pointed field map $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(u)\to X$ is such a monomorphism. Its henselian local ring is $\mathcal O_{X,x}^{h}=\varinjlim_{(U,u)}\Gamma(U,\mathcal O_U)$ over the cofiltered category of elementary étale neighborhoods, and it agrees with $\mathcal O_{U,u}^h$ for any one of them. A decent space's point-set $|X|$ is sober and admits a dense open schematic locus when it has finitely many irreducible components.

An algebraic space $X$ is *Jacobson* if it admits an étale surjective cover by Jacobson schemes. A topological space $|X|$ is Jacobson if closed points are dense in every closed subset. A *finite type point* $x\in X_{\mathrm{ft\text{-}pts}}$ is a point represented by a morphism from a field spectrum locally of finite type over $X$. A decent locally Noetherian algebraic space has a sober underlying topological space, and its specialization relations agree locally with those on elementary étale scheme charts.

hypotheses: Let $S$ be a locally Noetherian universally catenary scheme equipped with a dimension function $\delta:S\to\mathbf Z$. For any $S$-scheme $T$ locally of finite type, write $\delta_T(t)=\delta(f(t))+\operatorname{trdeg}_{\kappa(f(t))}\kappa(t)$; for integral closed $W\subset T$, let $\dim_\delta W=\delta_T(\eta_W)$.

A $q$-cycle on $T$ is a locally finite integral linear combination of integral closed subschemes of $\delta$-dimension $q$; $Z_q(T)$ is the group of these cycles. For a closed subscheme $W$ of dimension at most $q$, $[W]_q$ is the sum of the $q$-dimensional components weighted by generic-point length multiplicities. The Chow group $\mathrm{CH}_q(T)$ is $Z_q(T)$ modulo rational equivalence generated by locally finite principal divisors on integral closed subschemes of dimension $q+1$.

For a morphism $f:X\to Y$ and integer $p$, a bivariant class $c\in A^p(X\to Y)$ is a collection of homomorphisms $c_T:\mathrm{CH}_q(T)\to\mathrm{CH}_{q-p}(X\times_YT)$ indexed by $T\to Y$ and $q$, satisfying: (i) for proper $h:T'\to T$, $c_T(h_*\beta)=h_{X,*}c_{T'}(\beta)$; (ii) for flat $h$ of fixed relative dimension, $c_{T'}(h^*\alpha)=h_X^*c_T(\alpha)$; (iii) for $i:E\hookrightarrow T$ the zero scheme of a section of an invertible sheaf, $c_E(i^*\alpha)=i_X^*c_T(\alpha)$, with $h_X,i_X$ the base changes. Composition of families gives products $A^p(X\to Y)\times A^q(Y\to Z)\to A^{p+q}(X\to Z)$, and $A^*(X)=\bigoplus_pA^p(X\to X)$.

For a finite locally free sheaf $\mathcal E$ of rank $r$ on $X$, its operational Chern classes are $c_j(\mathcal E)\in A^j(X)$, with $c_0=1$, $c_j=0$ for $j>r$, and total class $c(\mathcal E)=\sum_jc_j(\mathcal E)$. For an integral closed $W\subset X$ of $\delta$-dimension $n$, the classes $c_j(\mathcal E|_W)\cap[W]$ in $\mathrm{CH}_{n-j}(W)$ are characterized via the projective bundle $\pi:\mathbf P(\mathcal E|_W)\to W$ with tautological quotient $\mathcal O(1)$ by $\sum_{i=0}^r(-1)^i c_1(\mathcal O(1))^i\cap\pi^*c_{r-i}=0$ with $c_0=[W]$. Extend to general cycles by sum and proper pushforward, then to Chow groups.

For a locally free $\mathcal E$ with formal Chern roots $x_1,\ldots,x_r$ (elementary symmetric polynomials equal to $c_i(\mathcal E)$), put $P_p(\mathcal E)=\sum_{j=1}^r x_j^p$, where $P_0=r$, and $\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal E)=\sum_{p\geq0}P_p(\mathcal E)/p!$. Each $P_p$ is the universal Newton polynomial in the Chern classes, and the degree-$p$ Chern character lies in $A^p(X)\otimes\mathbf Q$.

The derived category $D(\mathcal O_X)$ is the localization of complexes of $\mathcal O_X$-modules at quasi-isomorphisms. A perfect object is locally quasi-isomorphic to a bounded complex of finite locally free modules. A locally bounded complex is bounded in cohomological degrees locally on $X$; derived pullback is denoted $Lf^*$ and derived tensor product $\otimes^{\mathbf L}$.

For a bounded complex of finite locally free $\mathcal E^\bullet$, put $c(\mathcal E^\bullet)=\prod_n c(\mathcal E^n)^{(-1)^n}$ (formal multiplication and inversion in $\prod_{p\ge0}A^p(X)$), $P_p(\mathcal E^\bullet)=\sum_n(-1)^n P_p(\mathcal E^n)$ and $\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal E^\bullet)=\sum_n(-1)^n\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal E^n)$. For a locally bounded complex use this construction on open-and-closed pieces where the terms have constant rank and finitely many are nonzero. When the Chern classes of a perfect object $E$ are defined, these are the unique classes whose pullbacks to a suitable envelope agree with such a representing complex.

An envelope $f:Y\to X$ is a proper morphism such that every $x\in X$ has a preimage $y$ with $\kappa(y)\cong\kappa(x)$. We say Chern classes of a perfect object $E\in D(\mathcal O_X)$ are defined if an envelope $f:Y\to X$ exists such that $Lf^*E$ is represented by a locally bounded complex of finite locally free sheaves on $Y$.

records.statement:
A Noetherian local ring $A$ is *Gorenstein* if $A[0]$ is a dualizing complex (equivalently its self-injective dimension is finite). A general Noetherian ring is Gorenstein when all local rings are. An object of the derived category is *invertible* if it admits a two-sided derived-tensor inverse; locally it is a shift of a rank-one projective module. A *local complete intersection* map is locally a quotient of a polynomial algebra by a Koszul-regular sequence.

Let $A$ be a Noetherian ring.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $A$ has a dualizing complex $\omega_A^\bullet$, then
\begin{enumerate}
\item $A$ is Gorenstein $\Leftrightarrow$ $\omega_A^\bullet$ is an invertible
object of $D(A)$,
\item $A_\mathfrak p$ is Gorenstein $\Leftrightarrow$
$(\omega_A^\bullet)_\mathfrak p$ is an invertible object of
$D(A_\mathfrak p)$,
\item $\{\mathfrak p \in \Spec(A) \mid A_\mathfrak p\text{ is Gorenstein}\}$
is an open subset.
\end{enumerate}
\item If $A$ is Gorenstein, then $A$ has a dualizing complex if and
only if $A[0]$ is a dualizing complex.
\end{enumerate}

A derived-invertible object is locally a shift of an invertible module, not necessarily a module in degree zero.

morphisms of $S^{-1}\mathcal{C}$ which are the equivalence
classes of $(f : X' \to Y, s : X' \to X)$ and
$(g : X' \to Y, s : X' \to X)$. The following are equivalent
\begin{enumerate}
\item $A = B$,
\item there exists a morphism $t : X'' \to X'$ in $S$ with
$f \circ t = g \circ t$, and
\item there exists a morphism $a : X'' \to X'$ with
$f \circ a = g \circ a$ and $s \circ a \in S$.
\end{enumerate}

hypotheses: Let $S$ be a scheme and $X$ an algebraic space over $S$. Write $|X|$ for its underlying topological space, obtained from the equivalence classes of morphisms $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ from spectra of fields. The fibre product of algebraic spaces is understood in the category of algebraic spaces. For an étale presentation $U\to X$ by a scheme, $R=U\times_XU$ is its groupoid of arrows with projections $s,t:R\rightrightarrows U$. A morphism is representable if every base change along a map from a scheme has scheme source.

For $x\in|X|$, condition $(\alpha)_x$ means every affine étale morphism $U\to X$ has only finitely many points over $x$. Condition $(\beta)_x$ means there is a monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ representing $x$. Condition $(\gamma)_x$ means there is a quasi-compact monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ representing $x$, equivalently for every affine étale $U\to X$ both fibres over $x$ of $|U|\to|X|$ and $|U\times_XU|\to|X|$ are finite. The conditions $(\alpha),(\beta),(\gamma)$ mean the corresponding pointwise property holds at every $x$.

An algebraic space $X$ is *decent* when it satisfies $(\gamma)$, equivalently every point $x$ can be represented by a quasi-compact monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)\to X$. It is *reasonable* when it satisfies $(\delta)$, equivalently the fibres of every affine étale presentation $U\to X$ are universally bounded. It is *very reasonable* when it satisfies $(\epsilon)$, equivalently it has a Zariski-local quasi-compact surjective étale cover by schemes. The implications scheme or quasi-separated $\Rightarrow$ very reasonable $\Rightarrow$ reasonable $\Rightarrow$ decent hold.

A *residual space* $Z_x\to X$ at $x\in|X|$ is the unique monomorphism from a reduced locally Noetherian algebraic space with singleton underlying topology whose image is $x$ and which is universal among morphisms of such spaces into $X$ representing $x$. A space is *locally separated* if its diagonal is an immersion; it is quasi-separated if its diagonal is quasi-compact and quasi-separated. A locally Noetherian algebraic space is one with an étale cover by locally Noetherian schemes.

Let $S$ be locally Noetherian and universally catenary with dimension function $\delta:S\to\mathbf Z$. For $X$ locally of finite type over $S$, $\delta_X(x)=\delta(f(x))+\operatorname{trdeg}_{\kappa(f(x))}\kappa(x)$; $\dim_\delta(W)$ is its value at the generic point of integral $W$.

$Z_k(X)$ is the group of locally finite integer combinations of integral closed subschemes of $\delta$-dimension $k$. The cycle $[Z]_k$ of a closed subscheme $Z$ of dimension at most $k$ sums its $k$-dimensional components weighted by generic-point stalk lengths; $[\mathcal F]_k$ uses lengths of a coherent sheaf at the corresponding generic points of its support.

For a proper map $f:X\to Y$, $f_*[W]=0$ if $\dim_\delta f(W)<\dim_\delta W$, otherwise it is $[\kappa(\eta_W):\kappa(\eta_{f(W)})][f(W)]$. For flat $f$ of relative dimension $r$, the flat pullback of $[W]$ is the cycle $[X\times_Y W]_{\dim_\delta W+r}$ of the scheme-theoretic inverse image with component multiplicities.

$\mathrm{CH}_k(X)=Z_k(X)/\!\sim_{\mathrm{rat}}$, where rational equivalence is generated by locally finite sums of principal divisors of nonzero rational functions on integral closed subschemes of dimension $k+1$, pushed into $X$. An envelope is a proper map $f:Y\to X$ such that every $x\in X$ has some $y$ above it with $\kappa(y)\simeq\kappa(x)$.

$$

$$
in $Z_{n + r - 1}(X)$.

conclusions: The augmented Amitsur complex $0\to M\to A\otimes_RM\to A^{\otimes_R2}\otimes_RM\to\cdots$ is exact for every $M$.

$$0\to M\xrightarrow{u} A\otimes_R M\xrightarrow{d^0}A\otimes_R A\otimes_R M\xrightarrow{d^1}A^{\otimes_R3}\otimes_R M\to\cdots,$$

records.statement:
Let $S$ be a scheme.

Suppose given the following data:
\begin{enumerate}
\item For every $U \in \mathcal{B}$ a scheme $f_U : X_U \to U$ over $U$.
\item For $U, V \in \mathcal{B}$ with $V \subset U$ a morphism
$\rho^U_V : X_V \to X_U$ over $U$.
\end{enumerate}
Assume that
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] each $\rho^U_V$ induces an isomorphism
$X_V \to f_U^{-1}(V)$ of schemes over $V$,
\item[(b)] whenever $W, V, U \in \mathcal{B}$, with
$W \subset V \subset U$ we have $\rho^U_W = \rho^U_V \circ \rho ^V_W$.

Then there exists a morphism $f : X \to S$ of schemes
and isomorphisms $i_U : f^{-1}(U) \to X_U$ over $U \in \mathcal{B}$
such that for $V, U \in \mathcal{B}$ with $V \subset U$ the composition
$$
\xymatrix{
X_V \ar[r]^{i_V^{-1}} &
f^{-1}(V) \ar[rr]^{inclusion} & &
f^{-1}(U) \ar[r]^{i_U} &
X_U
}
$$
is the morphism $\rho^U_V$. Moreover $X$ is unique up to
unique isomorphism over $S$.

\item $F$ is exact if and only if for every short exact sequence
$0 \to A \to B \to C \to 0$

records.title: Lemma — Exact functor

conclusions: A unique isomorphism respecting all local normalizing identifications exists.
hypotheses: Finite-type T/S, fixed base dualizing D_S, fixed separated finite open cover U and normalized pairs including α_i.
records.statement: Fix a Noetherian scheme $S$ and a dualizing complex $D_S\in D(\mathcal O_S)$. For a finite-type $S$-scheme $T$, choose a finite open covering $\mathcal U=\{U_i\}$ by $S$-separated schemes, and let $p_i:U_i\to S$. Define $D_i=p_i^!D_S$, using the upper-shriek functors of separated finite-type schemes over $S$. On overlaps $U_{ij}$ their restrictions have canonical comparison isomorphisms $\varphi_{ij}:D_i|_{U_{ij}}\xrightarrow{\sim}D_j|_{U_{ij}}$ satisfying the cocycle condition on triple overlaps. A *dualizing complex normalized relative to $D_S$ and $\mathcal U$* is a pair $(D_T,\{\alpha_i\})$ with $D_T\in D(\mathcal O_T)$ and compatible isomorphisms $\alpha_i:D_T|_{U_i}\xrightarrow{\sim}D_i$, such that $\alpha_j\alpha_i^{-1}=\varphi_{ij}$ on each overlap. The normalized object includes the local identifications, not merely the derived isomorphism class of $D_T$. If two normalized pairs $(D_T,\{\alpha_i\})$ and $(D'_T,\{\alpha'_i\})$ exist for the *same* base complex $D_S$ and covering $\mathcal U$, then there exists a **unique** isomorphism $u:D_T\xrightarrow{\sim}D'_T$ in $D(\mathcal O_T)$ such that $\alpha'_i\circ u|_{U_i}=\alpha_i$ for every $i$. The uniqueness is relative to the specified normalizing isomorphisms, not a claim that the underlying dualizing complex has no automorphisms.

conclusions: Relative cup/evaluation/trace gives perfect field pairings for every cohomological degree.
hypotheses: X proper/k, D_X right-adjoint dualizing, E perfect, trace t.
records.statement:
Let $k$ be a field and $X$ a proper finite-type $k$-scheme of Krull dimension $d$. Let $p:X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ and let $a_p$ be the right adjoint to $Rp_*$ on $D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}$, where $Rp_*$ identifies with derived global sections $R\Gamma(X,-)$. Define the *canonical normalized dualizing complex* $D_X=a_p(k[0])$; it is the compactification-based $p^!k$. Put $\omega_X=H^{-d}(D_X)$ and let $t:H^0(X,D_X)\to k$ be the cohomological trace induced by the adjunction counit $R\Gamma(X,D_X)\to k$. Let $E\in D(\mathcal O_X)$ be a perfect complex, with derived dual $E^\vee=R\mathcal Hom_X(E,\mathcal O_X)$ and evaluation $\epsilon:E^\vee\otimes_X^{\mathbf L}E\to\mathcal O_X$. For each $i\in\mathbf Z$, the cup product, then evaluation, then trace $t$ defines a bilinear pairing
\[
H^i(X,D_X\otimes_X^{\mathbf L}E^\vee)\times H^{-i}(X,E)\to k.
\]
Each pairing is *perfect*: the two cohomology groups are finite-dimensional over $k$ and identify with each other's linear duals. The claim uses perfectness of $E$ and properness of $X$ and does not extend blindly to arbitrary unbounded quasi-coherent $E$.

records.title: Lemma — Compose base change

conclusions: The finite-syntomic de Rham trace exists, extends the algebra trace, satisfies the projection formula, and descends to relative de Rham complexes over any common base $S$.
hypotheses: $f:Y\to X$ is finite syntomic (and, for the final assertion, is over $S$).
records.statement:
Let $f:Y\to X$ be a finite syntomic morphism of schemes. There is a canonical trace morphism of absolute algebraic de Rham complexes
$$\Theta_{Y/X}:f_*\Omega^\bullet_{Y/\mathbf Z}\longrightarrow\Omega^\bullet_{X/\mathbf Z}$$
whose component in degree $0$ is the usual algebra trace $\operatorname{Tr}_f:f_*\mathcal O_Y\to\mathcal O_X$, and which satisfies the projection formula
$$\Theta_{Y/X}(f^*\omega\wedge\eta)=\omega\wedge\Theta_{Y/X}(\eta)$$
for local forms $\omega$ on $X$ and $\eta$ on $Y$. If $f$ is a morphism over a scheme $S$, this descends to a morphism of relative de Rham complexes
$$f_*\Omega^\bullet_{Y/S}\longrightarrow\Omega^\bullet_{X/S}.$$

records.title: Lemma — Properties system

hypotheses:
Let $f : X \to Y$ be a morphism of schemes locally of finite type over a
base scheme $S$. Let $x \in X$ be a point. Set $y = f(x)$ and assume
that $\kappa(y) = \kappa(x)$.
records.statement:
Let $f : X \to Y$ be a morphism of schemes locally of finite type over a
base scheme $S$. Let $x \in X$ be a point. Set $y = f(x)$ and assume
that $\kappa(y) = \kappa(x)$. Then the following are equivalent
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\text{d}f : T_{X/S, x} \longrightarrow T_{Y/S, y}$ is injective, and
\item $f$ is unramified at $x$.
\end{enumerate}

records.title: Lemma — Injective tangent spaces unramified

conclusions: The stated Mayer–Vietoris sequence beginning $0\to H^0(X,\mathcal F)\to H^0(U,\mathcal F)\oplus H^0(V,\mathcal F)\to H^0(U\cap V,\mathcal F)\to H^1(X,\mathcal F)\to\cdots$ is long exact and functorial in $\mathcal F$.
hypotheses: $X$ is a ringed space, $X=U\cup V$ with $U,V$ open, and $\mathcal F$ is an $\mathcal O_X$-module.
records.statement:
Let $X$ be a ringed space. Suppose that $X = U \cup V$ is a
union of two open subsets. For every $\mathcal{O}_X$-module $\mathcal{F}$
there exists a long exact cohomology sequence
$$
0 \to
H^0(X, \mathcal{F}) \to
H^0(U, \mathcal{F}) \oplus H^0(V, \mathcal{F}) \to
H^0(U \cap V, \mathcal{F}) \to
H^1(X, \mathcal{F}) \to \ldots
$$
This long exact sequence is functorial in $\mathcal{F}$.

records.title: Lemma — Mayer vietoris

conclusions:
If $n\in \mathcal{O}_S^*$ then
$$
0 \to
\mu_{n, S} \to
\mathbf{G}_{m, S} \xrightarrow{(\cdot)^n}
\mathbf{G}_{m, S} \to 0
$$
is a short exact sequence of sheaves on both the small and
big \'etale site of $S$.
The last power map G_m→G_m is a **surjection of étale sheaves**, shown by an étale **finite locally free** cover adjoining an nth root of a unit (derivative nT^{n−1} invertible). If n is not invertible this exactness can fail in étale topology; only fppf/syntomic version remains valid without inversion.
hypotheses:
Fix a scheme $S$. The **big $\tau$-site** $(\mathrm{Sch}/S)_\tau$ is a small-universe-selected category of $S$-schemes with covering families of type $\tau\in\{\mathrm{fppf},\mathrm{syntomic},\mathrm{smooth},\mathrm{\acute etale},\mathrm{Zariski}\}$. The **small étale site** $S_{\acute etale}$ has as objects étale $S$-schemes and as covers jointly surjective étale families; the **small Zariski site** $S_{\mathrm{Zar}}$ has open subschemes as objects. These are different sites; restriction from a big to a small site is not an identity of categories. For an abelian sheaf $\mathcal F$ on a site, $H^p_\tau(U,\mathcal F)$ denotes the $p$-th right derived functor of its sections over the site object $U$. A *standard $\tau$-cover of an affine $U$* is a **finite** jointly surjective family of affine maps $U_i\to U$, each flat finitely presented for fppf, standard syntomic, standard smooth, étale, or standard principal-open immersion, respectively.

On the small or big étale site of a scheme $S$, $\mathbf G_{m,S}(U)=\Gamma(U,\mathcal O_U^\times)$ is the *units sheaf*, and $\mu_{n,S}(U)=\{u\in\Gamma(U,\mathcal O_U^\times):u^n=1\}$ the *$n$th roots of unity* sheaf (representable by the group scheme $\mu_n$). The notation $n\in\mathcal O_S^\times$ means the image of the positive integer $n$ is a unit in the structure sheaf **everywhere on $S$**. A short exact sequence of sheaves means the final map is locally surjective in that site, not necessarily surjective on each group of global sections.

conclusions:

Let $\mathcal S_X(U)$ be the regular functions acting injectively on $\mathcal O_U$ as a sheaf. Write $\mathcal K_X$ for the sheafification of $U\mapsto\mathcal S_X(U)^{-1}\mathcal O_X(U)$ and $\mathcal K_X(\mathcal F)=\mathcal F\otimes\mathcal K_X$; a meromorphic section is a global section of this sheaf. For an invertible $\mathcal L$, such a section is regular if multiplication $\mathcal K_X\to\mathcal K_X(\mathcal L)$ is injective. Pullback of meromorphic functions is defined for $f:X\to Y$ when restrictions of $f^\sharp$ send every regular section on Y to a regular section on X. The denominator ideal of $s$ is $\mathcal I(V)=\{a\in\mathcal O_X(V):as\in\mathcal L(V)\}$. For a global function h, $X_h=\{x:h_x\notin\mathfrak m_x\}$. Let $f : X \to Y$ be a morphism of locally ringed spaces.
Assume that pullbacks of meromorphic functions are defined
for $f$ (see
Definition \ref{definition-pullback-meromorphic-sections}).
\begin{enumerate}
\item Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a sheaf of $\mathcal{O}_Y$-modules.
There is a canonical pullback map
$f^* : \Gamma(Y, \mathcal{K}_Y(\mathcal{F})) \to
\Gamma(X, \mathcal{K}_X(f^*\mathcal{F}))$
for meromorphic sections of $\mathcal{F}$.
\item Let $\mathcal{L}$ be an invertible $\mathcal{O}_Y$-module.
A regular meromorphic section $s$ of $\mathcal{L}$ pulls back
to a regular meromorphic section $f^*s$ of $f^*\mathcal{L}$.
\end{enumerate}

records.title: Lemma — Tensor products commute with limits

conclusions: Acyclic dg A-modules form a strictly full saturated triangulated subcategory Ac; quasi-isomorphisms form the associated saturated multiplicative system, the kernel of localization Q is Ac, and H⁰ factors through Q.
hypotheses: (A,d) is a dg algebra; consider its dg-module homotopy category.
records.statement:
Let $(A, \text{d})$ be a differential graded algebra.
The full subcategory $\text{Ac}$ of $K(\text{Mod}_{(A, \text{d})})$
consisting of acyclic modules is a strictly full saturated triangulated
subcategory of $K(\text{Mod}_{(A, \text{d})})$.
The corresponding saturated multiplicative system

of $K(\text{Mod}_{(A, \text{d})})$ is the class $\text{Qis}$
of quasi-isomorphisms. In particular, the kernel of the localization
functor
$$
Q : K(\text{Mod}_{(A, \text{d})}) \to
\text{Qis}^{-1}K(\text{Mod}_{(A, \text{d})})
$$
is $\text{Ac}$. Moreover, the functor $H^0$ factors through $Q$.

hypotheses: For a scheme $T$ locally of finite type over a field $k$, $Z_n(T)$ is the group of locally finite integral linear combinations of integral closed subschemes of Krull dimension $n$, and $\mathrm{CH}_n(T)$ is $Z_n(T)$ modulo rational equivalence generated by principal divisors on integral closed subschemes of dimension $n+1$. If $A\subset T$ has dimension at most $n$, write $[A]_n$ for its cycle of $n$-dimensional components weighted by lengths of the local rings at generic points.

Let $k$ be a field, and let $X,Y$ be schemes locally of finite type over $k$. Define exterior product on cycles by $[W]\times[V]=[W\times_k V]_{\dim W+\dim V}$ for integral closed $W\subset X$, $V\subset Y$, extending bilinearly, where $[W\times_kV]$ uses generic-point multiplicities even if this product is reducible or nonreduced.

For a morphism $f:T\to U$, a degree-$p$ bivariant class $c\in A^p(T\to U)$ consists of homomorphisms $\mathrm{CH}_n(U')\to\mathrm{CH}_{n-p}(T\times_UU')$ for all $U'\to U$ of locally finite type, compatible with proper pushforwards, flat pullbacks of fixed relative dimension, and Gysin maps for zero schemes of invertible-sheaf sections. Products of bivariant classes are composition of their compatible families after base change.

Let $X$ be smooth over a field $k$. Its diagonal $\Delta:X\hookrightarrow X\times_kX$ is a regular immersion and has a Gysin class $\Delta^!$. For schemes $U,V$ locally of finite type over $X$, define intersection of Chow classes by $\alpha\cdot\beta:=\Delta^!(\alpha\times\beta)\in\mathrm{CH}_*(U\times_XV)$; for $X$ smooth of pure dimension $d$, $\mathrm{CH}_n(U)\cdot\mathrm{CH}_m(V)\subseteq\mathrm{CH}_{n+m-d}(U\times_XV)$. For $U=V=X$ this defines the intersection product on $\mathrm{CH}_*(X)$.

For a local complete intersection morphism $f:U\to V$ that has a global factorization $U\xrightarrow{i}P\xrightarrow{g}V$ with $i$ a regular immersion and $g$ smooth, its Gysin class is $f^!=i^!\circ g^*$, independent of the factorization. A smooth $k$-morphism between smooth $k$-schemes is lci; the morphisms between smooth $k$-schemes in the statements below have such Gysin classes. On a regular closed immersion $i:W\hookrightarrow T$, $i^!$ is the Gysin pullback of bivariant intersection theory.

Let $k$ be a field. Let $X$ be an integral scheme smooth over $k$.
Let $Y, Z \subset X$ be integral closed subschemes. Set
$d = \dim(Y) + \dim(Z) - \dim(X)$. Assume
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\dim(Y \cap Z) \leq d$, and
\item $\mathcal{O}_{Y, \xi}$ and $\mathcal{O}_{Z, \xi}$

hypotheses: (C,O) is a ringed site, U∈C, and α:E^bullet→F^bullet, f:G^bullet→F^bullet are chain maps.
E^bullet is strictly perfect and E^j=0 for j<a.
H^j(f) is an isomorphism for j>a and surjective for j=a.
records.statement:
For any ringed site (C,O), a **strictly perfect complex** E^bullet is a **bounded** complex whose every term is a direct summand of a finite free O-module (source Definition strictly-perfect at 11716–11724). For U∈C a strictly perfect complex on (C/U,O_U) uses the restricted ring; a finite locally projective module is not being assumed globally free. In the source diagram α:E^bullet→F^bullet is the given map, f:G^bullet→F^bullet the vertical map and a dotted E^bullet→G^bullet is to be constructed **up to homotopy after a covering**. No global lift or strict commutativity is asserted.

Let $(\mathcal{C}, \mathcal{O})$ be a ringed site. Let $U$ be an object of
$\mathcal{C}$. Given a solid diagram of complexes of $\mathcal{O}_U$-modules
$$
\xymatrix{
\mathcal{E}^\bullet \ar@{..>}[dr] \ar[r]_\alpha & \mathcal{F}^\bullet \\
& \mathcal{G}^\bullet \ar[u]_f
}
$$
with $\mathcal{E}^\bullet$ strictly perfect, $\mathcal{E}^j = 0$ for
$j < a$ and $H^j(f)$ an isomorphism for $j > a$ and surjective for
$j = a$, then there exists a covering $\{U_i \to U\}$ and for each $i$
a dotted arrow over $U_i$ making the diagram commute up to homotopy.
