hypotheses: A curve over a field $k$ means an integral separated $k$-scheme of finite type and Krull dimension $1$. A normal (equivalently, nonsingular or regular) curve has regular local rings; its local rings at closed points are discrete valuation rings. A rational map of integral $k$-varieties is an equivalence class of morphisms defined on dense open subschemes, and it is dominant if it maps generic points to generic points. A proper normal curve has a unique nonsingular projective model (the regular proper curve with the same function field). The function field of a curve $X$ is $k(X)=\kappa(\eta_X)$.

Suppose $\operatorname{char}k=p>0$. The $n$-fold Frobenius twist of a $k$-scheme $X$ is $X^{(p^n)}=X\times_{\operatorname{Spec}k,F_k^n}\operatorname{Spec}k$, and $F_{X/k}^n:X\to X^{(p^n)}$ is its relative $n$-fold Frobenius morphism. For a smooth curve it is finite purely inseparable of degree $p^n$ (for $n\ge0$). A morphism of proper integral curves is nonconstant if its function-field homomorphism is injective and not just an extension of constants.

For a proper $k$-scheme $X$ of dimension $1$ with $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X)=k$, its genus is $g(X)=\dim_kH^1(X,\mathcal O_X)$ and $\chi(X,\mathcal O_X)=1-g(X)$. Such an $X$ is connected, Cohen–Macaulay, and equidimensional of dimension $1$; its dualizing module is $\omega_X=H^{-1}(f^!k)$ and satisfies $H^1(X,\omega_X)\cong k$. For a smooth proper curve, $\omega_X\simeq\Omega_{X/k}$; if $X$ is Gorenstein, $\omega_X$ is invertible.

records.statement:
Let $\Sch_{smooth}$ be a big smooth site as in
Definition \ref{definition-big-smooth-site}.
Let $T \in \Ob(\Sch_{smooth})$.
Let $\{T_i \to T\}_{i \in I}$ be an arbitrary smooth covering of $T$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item There exists a covering $\{U_j \to T\}_{j \in J}$ of $T$ in the site
$\Sch_{smooth}$ which refines $\{T_i \to T\}_{i \in I}$.
\item If $\{T_i \to T\}_{i \in I}$ is a standard smooth covering, then
it is tautologically equivalent to a covering of $\Sch_{smooth}$.
\item If $\{T_i \to T\}_{i \in I}$ is a Zariski covering, then
it is tautologically equivalent to a covering of $\Sch_{smooth}$.
\end{enumerate}
Two families over the same target are tautologically equivalent when there are maps between their index sets in both directions and isomorphisms over the target from each source object to the corresponding source object in the other family.

records.title: Lemma — Pi0 profinite

conclusions: a_f preserves bounded-below cohomology, with a uniform lower cohomological bound.
hypotheses: f qcqs; a_f right adjoint to Rf_*.
records.statement: Let $D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}(\mathcal O_T)$ be the unbounded derived category of complexes of $\mathcal O_T$-modules having quasi-coherent cohomology sheaves. For a morphism $f:X\to Y$ of quasi-compact and quasi-separated schemes, denote by $a_f:D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}(\mathcal O_Y)\to D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}(\mathcal O_X)$ the right adjoint to the derived pushforward $Rf_*$. Thus $\operatorname{Hom}_X(E,a_f(K))\cong\operatorname{Hom}_Y(Rf_*E,K)$ naturally in $E,K$, with unit $\eta_f:\mathrm{id}\to a_f Rf_*$ and counit $\operatorname{Tr}_f:Rf_*a_f\to\mathrm{id}$. This right adjoint is not in general the Grothendieck upper-shriek functor $f^!$. There exists an integer $N$ depending only on $f$ such that for every $K\in D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}(\mathcal O_Y)$ and integer $c$, if $H^i(K)=0$ for every $i\le c$, then $H^i(a_f(K))=0$ for every $i\le c-N$. In particular $a_f$ carries $D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}^+(\mathcal O_Y)$ into $D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}^+(\mathcal O_X)$.

conclusions:
The map $L_{B/A} \to L_{B/A}$
of Section \ref{section-functoriality} induced by the
Frobenius maps $F_A$ and $F_B$ is homotopic to zero.
hypotheses: For a ring map $A\to B$, let $\Omega_{B/A}$ be the module of Kähler differentials. The cotangent complex $L_{B/A}\in D(B)$ is obtained from the standard augmented simplicial polynomial $A$-algebra resolution $P_\bullet\to B$, where $P_0=A[B]$, $P_1=A[A[B]]$, etc., by taking the chain complex (in nonpositive cohomological degrees) associated to the simplicial $B$-module $\Omega_{P_\bullet/A}\otimes_{P_\bullet}B$. Here $A[E]$ denotes the polynomial algebra freely generated by a set $E$, $D(B)$ is the derived category of $B$-modules, and $H^i$ denotes degree-$i$ cohomology.

A quasi-isomorphism is a map of complexes inducing an isomorphism on every cohomology module. We write $M[0]$ for a module concentrated in degree zero, $M[1]$ for a module in degree $-1$, $\otimes_A^{\mathbf L}$ for derived tensor product, and $\tau_{\geq -1}$ for the standard truncation in cohomological degrees at least $-1$. The module $\Omega_{B/A}$ is generated by symbols $db$ subject to additivity, the Leibniz rule, and $da=0$ for $a\in A$.

For a characteristic-$p$ ring $A$ ($p$ prime), the Frobenius endomorphism is $F_A(a)=a^p$. Given a characteristic-$p$ ring map $A\to B$, its Frobenius square $(F_A,F_B)$ induces maps on the functorial simplicial standard resolution $P_\bullet$ and the cotangent complex $L_{B/A}$; these maps are generally semilinear over $B$ under $F_B$. A homotopy of simplicial maps means simplicial homotopy, and a chain homotopy on a complex induces the same map in its derived category.
records.statement:
For a ring map $A\to B$, let $\Omega_{B/A}$ be the module of Kähler differentials. The cotangent complex $L_{B/A}\in D(B)$ is obtained from the standard augmented simplicial polynomial $A$-algebra resolution $P_\bullet\to B$, where $P_0=A[B]$, $P_1=A[A[B]]$, etc., by taking the chain complex (in nonpositive cohomological degrees) associated to the simplicial $B$-module $\Omega_{P_\bullet/A}\otimes_{P_\bullet}B$. Here $A[E]$ denotes the polynomial algebra freely generated by a set $E$, $D(B)$ is the derived category of $B$-modules, and $H^i$ denotes degree-$i$ cohomology.

A quasi-isomorphism is a map of complexes inducing an isomorphism on every cohomology module. We write $M[0]$ for a module concentrated in degree zero, $M[1]$ for a module in degree $-1$, $\otimes_A^{\mathbf L}$ for derived tensor product, and $\tau_{\geq -1}$ for the standard truncation in cohomological degrees at least $-1$. The module $\Omega_{B/A}$ is generated by symbols $db$ subject to additivity, the Leibniz rule, and $da=0$ for $a\in A$.

For a characteristic-$p$ ring $A$ ($p$ prime), the Frobenius endomorphism is $F_A(a)=a^p$. Given a characteristic-$p$ ring map $A\to B$, its Frobenius square $(F_A,F_B)$ induces maps on the functorial simplicial standard resolution $P_\bullet$ and the cotangent complex $L_{B/A}$; these maps are generally semilinear over $B$ under $F_B$. A homotopy of simplicial maps means simplicial homotopy, and a chain homotopy on a complex induces the same map in its derived category.

Let $p$ be a prime number. Let $A \to B$ be a ring homomorphism
and assume that $p = 0$ in $A$. The map $L_{B/A} \to L_{B/A}$
induced by the natural Frobenius square of ring maps induced by the
Frobenius maps $F_A$ and $F_B$ is homotopic to zero.

records.title: Lemma — Image connected space

conclusions: Every τ descent datum of P-type schemes is effective.
hypotheses: P is base-change stable, finite-coproduct stable, and affine-singleton descent effective for the indicated τ-coverings.
records.statement:
Let $\mathcal P$ be a property of morphisms of schemes over a base, and let $\tau\in\{\mathrm{fpqc},\mathrm{fppf},\mathrm{\acute etale},\mathrm{smooth},\mathrm{syntomic}\}$. Say that *morphisms of type $\mathcal P$ satisfy descent for $\tau$-coverings* if, for every $\tau$-covering $\{U_i\to S\}$, every scheme descent datum $(X_i,\varphi_{ij})$ with each $X_i\to U_i$ having $\mathcal P$ is effective, i.e. isomorphic to the canonical pullback descent datum of some $S$-scheme.

Suppose (1) $\mathcal P$ is preserved by arbitrary base change; (2) $\mathcal P$ is preserved by finite disjoint unions of morphisms, so that if $Y_j\to V_j$ have $\mathcal P$ for $1\leq j\leq m$, then $\coprod_jY_j\to\coprod_jV_j$ has $\mathcal P$; and (3) for each surjective map of affine schemes $X\to S$ of the corresponding class—flat for fpqc, flat and of finite presentation for fppf, étale for étale, smooth for smooth, and syntomic for syntomic—every descent datum $(V,\varphi)$ for $X/S$ with $V\to X$ having $\mathcal P$ is effective. Then morphisms of type $\mathcal P$ satisfy descent for all $\tau$-coverings. This asserts effectivity of the descent datum; the definition does not separately assert that its descended morphism has $\mathcal P$.

\longrightarrow
\text{Mod}^{dg}_{(A, \text{d})}
$$
of differential graded categories. This functor induces functors
$$
\text{Mod}_{(B, \text{d})} \to \text{Mod}_{(A, \text{d})}
\quad\text{and}\quad
K(\text{Mod}_{(B, \text{d})}) \to K(\text{Mod}_{(A, \text{d})})

records.title: Lemma — Pushforward composition

conclusions: Pullback along f on DD(X/S) is naturally isomorphic to the identity.
hypotheses: f is an S-selfmap of X.
records.statement: Fix $p:X\to S$. Write $\mathrm{DD}(X/S)$ for the category of descent data for schemes along $X\to S$. An object is a scheme $V\to X$ and an isomorphism $\varphi:V\times_S X\xrightarrow{\sim} X\times_SV$ over $X\times_SX$ satisfying the cocycle identity on $X\times_SX\times_SX$. Morphisms are $X$-morphisms compatible with these isomorphisms. For a morphism $f:X'\to X$ over $S$, pullback is the functor $f^*:\mathrm{DD}(X/S)\to\mathrm{DD}(X'/S)$ taking $V$ to $V\times_X X'$ and $\varphi$ to its pullback along $f\times_Sf$. If $f:X\to X$ is any morphism over $S$, then $f^*:\mathrm{DD}(X/S)\to\mathrm{DD}(X/S)$ is naturally isomorphic to the identity functor. The isomorphism uses the descent datum to identify changes of the chosen presentation map $X\to S$.

records.title: Lemma — Coherent projective

conclusions: $X$ is a scheme.
$X \cong \Spec(k)$ for some field $k$.
hypotheses: Let $S$ be a scheme and $X$ an algebraic space over $S$. Write $|X|$ for its underlying topological space, obtained from the equivalence classes of morphisms $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ from spectra of fields. The fibre product of algebraic spaces is understood in the category of algebraic spaces. For an étale presentation $U\to X$ by a scheme, $R=U\times_XU$ is its groupoid of arrows with projections $s,t:R\rightrightarrows U$. A morphism is representable if every base change along a map from a scheme has scheme source.

For $x\in|X|$, condition $(\alpha)_x$ means every affine étale morphism $U\to X$ has only finitely many points over $x$. Condition $(\beta)_x$ means there is a monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ representing $x$. Condition $(\gamma)_x$ means there is a quasi-compact monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ representing $x$, equivalently for every affine étale $U\to X$ both fibres over $x$ of $|U|\to|X|$ and $|U\times_XU|\to|X|$ are finite. The conditions $(\alpha),(\beta),(\gamma)$ mean the corresponding pointwise property holds at every $x$.

An algebraic space $X$ is *decent* when it satisfies $(\gamma)$, equivalently every point $x$ can be represented by a quasi-compact monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)\to X$. It is *reasonable* when it satisfies $(\delta)$, equivalently the fibres of every affine étale presentation $U\to X$ are universally bounded. It is *very reasonable* when it satisfies $(\epsilon)$, equivalently it has a Zariski-local quasi-compact surjective étale cover by schemes. The implications scheme or quasi-separated $\Rightarrow$ very reasonable $\Rightarrow$ reasonable $\Rightarrow$ decent hold.

A *residual space* $Z_x\to X$ at $x\in|X|$ is the unique monomorphism from a reduced locally Noetherian algebraic space with singleton underlying topology whose image is $x$ and which is universal among morphisms of such spaces into $X$ representing $x$. A space is *locally separated* if its diagonal is an immersion; it is quasi-separated if its diagonal is quasi-compact and quasi-separated. A locally Noetherian algebraic space is one with an étale cover by locally Noetherian schemes.

For points $a,b$ of a topological space, $b\leadsto a$ means $a\in\overline{\{b\}}$, i.e., $a$ is a specialization of $b$. The space is $T_0$ (Kolmogorov) when distinct points have distinct closures, and sober when every irreducible closed subset has exactly one generic point. A subset is locally constructible if its intersection with every quasi-compact open subset is a finite union of locally closed subsets. An algebraic space has a locally constructible subset in the étale sense when its inverse image in every étale scheme chart is locally constructible.

Let $S$ be a scheme and $X$ an algebraic space over $S$. Write $|X|$ for its underlying topological space, obtained from the equivalence classes of morphisms $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ from spectra of fields. The fibre product of algebraic spaces is understood in the category of algebraic spaces. For an étale presentation $U\to X$ by a scheme, $R=U\times_XU$ is its groupoid of arrows with projections $s,t:R\rightrightarrows U$. A morphism is representable if every base change along a map from a scheme has scheme source.

For $x\in|X|$, condition $(\alpha)_x$ means every affine étale morphism $U\to X$ has only finitely many points over $x$. Condition $(\beta)_x$ means there is a monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ representing $x$. Condition $(\gamma)_x$ means there is a quasi-compact monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ representing $x$, equivalently for every affine étale $U\to X$ both fibres over $x$ of $|U|\to|X|$ and $|U\times_XU|\to|X|$ are finite. The conditions $(\alpha),(\beta),(\gamma)$ mean the corresponding pointwise property holds at every $x$.

An algebraic space $X$ is *decent* when it satisfies $(\gamma)$, equivalently every point $x$ can be represented by a quasi-compact monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)\to X$. It is *reasonable* when it satisfies $(\delta)$, equivalently the fibres of every affine étale presentation $U\to X$ are universally bounded. It is *very reasonable* when it satisfies $(\epsilon)$, equivalently it has a Zariski-local quasi-compact surjective étale cover by schemes. The implications scheme or quasi-separated $\Rightarrow$ very reasonable $\Rightarrow$ reasonable $\Rightarrow$ decent hold.

A *residual space* $Z_x\to X$ at $x\in|X|$ is the unique monomorphism from a reduced locally Noetherian algebraic space with singleton underlying topology whose image is $x$ and which is universal among morphisms of such spaces into $X$ representing $x$. A space is *locally separated* if its diagonal is an immersion; it is quasi-separated if its diagonal is quasi-compact and quasi-separated. A locally Noetherian algebraic space is one with an étale cover by locally Noetherian schemes.

For points $a,b$ of a topological space, $b\leadsto a$ means $a\in\overline{\{b\}}$, i.e., $a$ is a specialization of $b$. The space is $T_0$ (Kolmogorov) when distinct points have distinct closures, and sober when every irreducible closed subset has exactly one generic point. A subset is locally constructible if its intersection with every quasi-compact open subset is a finite union of locally closed subsets. An algebraic space has a locally constructible subset in the étale sense when its inverse image in every étale scheme chart is locally constructible.

Let $S$ be a scheme. Let $X$ be a decent algebraic space over $S$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $|X|$ is a singleton then $X$ is a scheme.
\item If $|X|$ is a singleton and $X$ is reduced, then
$X \cong \operatorname{Spec}(k)$ for some field $k$.
\end{enumerate}

On a local ring $(A,\mathfrak m,\kappa)$ it is *normalized* if $R\operatorname{Hom}_A(\kappa,\omega_A^\bullet)\simeq\kappa[0]$. Its canonical module is $H^{-\dim A}(\omega_A^\bullet)$. A dualizing complex $\omega_A^\bullet$ over a Noetherian ring is a bounded coherent complex of finite injective dimension with $A\simeq R\operatorname{Hom}_A(\omega_A^\bullet,\omega_A^\bullet)$. On a local ring $(A,\mathfrak m,\kappa)$ it is *normalized* if $R\operatorname{Hom}_A(\kappa,\omega_A^\bullet)\simeq\kappa[0]$. Its canonical module is $H^{-\dim A}(\omega_A^\bullet)$. A local ring is *Cohen–Macaulay* if its depth equals Krull dimension; a finite module is Cohen–Macaulay if depth equals dimension of its support.

Let $(A, \mathfrak m, \kappa)$ be a Noetherian local ring
with normalized dualizing complex $\omega_A^\bullet$
and dualizing module $\omega_A = H^{-\dim(A)}(\omega_A^\bullet)$.
The following are equivalent
\begin{enumerate}
\item $A$ is Cohen-Macaulay,
\item $\omega_A^\bullet$ is concentrated in a single degree, and
\item $\omega_A^\bullet = \omega_A[\dim(A)]$.
\end{enumerate}
In this case $\omega_A$ is a maximal Cohen-Macaulay module.

A maximal Cohen–Macaulay module has depth equal to dim A.

\to \mathcal{O}_{X \cap Y} \to 0

$$
\xymatrix{
X \cap Y \ar[r] \ar[d] & X \ar[d] \\
Y \ar[r] & X \cup Y
}

is cocartesian in the category of schemes, i.e.,
$X \cup Y = X \amalg_{X \cap Y} Y$.

conclusions: Nonzero cohomology of f^!O_Y can occur only in degrees at least minus the fibre dimension.
hypotheses: f in FTS_S, x∈X, y=f(x), fibre dimension at x defined.
records.statement:
Fix a Noetherian base $S$. Write $\mathrm{FTS}_S$ for separated schemes of finite type over $S$, with $S$-morphisms. For $f:X\to Y$ in $\mathrm{FTS}_S$, choose a factorization $f=\bar f\circ j$ with $j:X\hookrightarrow\bar X$ an open immersion and $\bar f:\bar X\to Y$ proper. If $a_{\bar f}$ is the right adjoint to $R\bar f_*$ on unbounded quasi-coherent derived categories, define $f^!:D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}^+(\mathcal O_Y)\to D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}^+(\mathcal O_X)$ as $j^*a_{\bar f}$, independently (up to canonical identifications) of the chosen compactification. For a dualizing complex $D_T$ on a locally Noetherian scheme $T$, its associated dimension function $\delta_T:T\to\mathbf Z$ assigns to $t$ the unique integer such that the stalk $D_{T,t}[-\delta_T(t)]$ is a *normalized* dualizing complex over $\mathcal O_{T,t}$, i.e. $R\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O_{T,t}}(\kappa(t),D_{T,t}[-\delta_T(t)])\simeq\kappa(t)[0]$. For $x\in X$ above $y\in Y$, let $X_y=X\times_Y\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(y)$ be the fibre and $\dim_x(X_y)$ its local topological dimension at $x$ (minimum dimension of neighbourhoods in the fibre). Let $x\in X$, $y=f(x)$. If $H^i(f^!\mathcal O_Y)_x$ is nonzero, then
\[
i\ge-\dim_x(X_y).
\]
This is a lower bound for degrees of the upper-shriek structure complex; without extra hypotheses there is no asserted universal upper bound.

hypotheses: Let $(R,\mathfrak m,\kappa)$ be a local ring and $M$ a finite-length $R$-module of length $\ell$. An admissible sequence is an $\ell$-tuple $(e_1,\ldots,e_\ell)$ with $\mathfrak m e_i\subseteq\sum_{j<i}Re_j$. The determinant line $\det_\kappa(M)$ is the $\kappa$-space generated by symbols $[e_1,\ldots,e_\ell]$ modulo: (i) a symbol is zero if any $e_i\in\sum_{j<i}Re_j$; (ii) replacing $e_i$ by $\lambda e_i'+x$ with $x\in\sum_{j<i}Re_j$ and $\lambda\in R^\times$ scales the symbol by $\bar\lambda$; (iii) exchanging adjacent $e_{i-1},e_i$ changes the sign when $\mathfrak m e_i\subseteq\sum_{j<i-1}Re_j$. This line is one-dimensional. An isomorphism $h:M\to N$ induces $\det_\kappa(h)$ by applying $h$ to admissible symbols. For a short exact sequence $0\to K\to L\to N\to0$, the canonical determinant isomorphism $\gamma_{K\to L\to N}:\det_\kappa K\otimes_\kappa\det_\kappa N\xrightarrow{\sim}\det_\kappa L$ concatenates an admissible sequence of $K$ with chosen lifts of one from $N$; it is natural under isomorphisms of exact sequences.

For finite-length $R$-module $M$ and endomorphisms $\varphi,\psi:M\to M$ with $\varphi\psi=\psi\varphi=0$ and $\ker\varphi=\operatorname{im}\psi$, $\ker\psi=\operatorname{im}\varphi$, call $(M,\varphi,\psi)$ an exact $(2,1)$-periodic complex. With $I_\varphi=\operatorname{im}\varphi$, $I_\psi=\operatorname{im}\psi$, put $K_\varphi=\ker\varphi=I_\psi$, $K_\psi=\ker\psi=I_\varphi$. Let $\gamma_\varphi:\det K_\varphi\otimes\det I_\varphi\to\det M$, $\gamma_\psi:\det K_\psi\otimes\det I_\psi\to\det M$ be the determinant isomorphisms and $\sigma$ swap the tensor factors. Define $\det_\kappa(M,\varphi,\psi)\in\kappa^\times$ as the unique scalar such that $\gamma_\psi\circ\sigma\circ\gamma_\varphi^{-1}$ acts on $\det M$ by $(-1)^{\ell(I_\varphi)\ell(I_\psi)}\det_\kappa(M,\varphi,\psi)$.

For a one-dimensional Noetherian local domain $A$, use $d_A(a,b)$ for the special case $M=A$, and write $\operatorname{ord}_A(b)=\operatorname{length}_A(A/bA)$ for a nonzero nonunit $b$ (extended with value zero for units).

hypotheses: Let $A'\twoheadrightarrow A$ be a surjective homomorphism of commutative rings with square-zero kernel $I$; let $A\to B$ be an $A$-algebra, $N$ a $B$-module, and $c:I\to N$ an $A$-linear map. A solution of the lifting problem is a commutative diagram of ring homomorphisms with exact rows $0\to I\to A'\to A\to0$ and $0\to N\to B'\to B\to0$ in which $N\subset B'$ is square-zero, $B'$ is an $A'$-algebra and the induced map $I\to N$ equals $c$. Isomorphisms of solutions commute with the maps from $A'$ and to $B$ and are the identity on the identified $N$.

For a homomorphism of rings $A\to B$ choose a polynomial presentation $P=A[E]\twoheadrightarrow B$ with kernel $J$. The naive cotangent complex $\mathrm{NL}_{B/A}$ is the two-term complex $(J/J^2\xrightarrow{d}\Omega_{P/A}\otimes_PB)$ in cohomological degrees $-1,0$, well defined up to quasi-isomorphism. The module of Kähler differentials $\Omega_{B/A}$ is its $H^0$. The notation $\operatorname{Ext}_B^q(K,N)$ means $\operatorname{Hom}_{D(B)}(K,N[q])$. For ringed spaces, topoi, and schemes, $\mathrm{NL}$ denotes the corresponding locally defined complex of sheaves of modules.

records.title: Lemma — Locally projective pushforward

conclusions: Derived Hom comparison and all Ext^i base-change maps are isomorphisms.
hypotheses: A→B flat with A/I≈B/IB; K torsion-cohomology and L arbitrary.
records.statement:
Let $A$ be a commutative ring, $I=(f_1,\ldots,f_r)\subseteq A$ finitely generated, and $Z=V(I)\subseteq\operatorname{Spec}A$. Let $D_{\mathcal T_I}(A)\subseteq D(A)$ be the full triangulated subcategory of complexes whose cohomology modules are $I$-power torsion. Let $C_A(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$ be the *augmented alternating Čech complex* $[A\to\bigoplus_i A_{f_i}\to\bigoplus_{i<j}A_{f_if_j}\to\cdots\to A_{f_1\cdots f_r}]$, with $A$ in degree $0$, the standard alternating restriction differentials, and all terms flat. Define $R\Gamma_Z(K)=C_A(f_1,\ldots,f_r)\otimes_A^{\mathbf L}K\in D_{\mathcal T_I}(A)$, the right adjoint to the inclusion $D_{\mathcal T_I}(A)\hookrightarrow D(A)$. This is local cohomology, unlike $R\Gamma_I$ above for general non-Noetherian $A$. Let $A\to B$ be flat with $A/I\xrightarrow{\sim}B/IB$. If $K\in D_{\mathcal T_I}(A)$ and $L\in D(A)$, then the canonical map
\[
R\operatorname{Hom}_A(K,L)\xrightarrow{\sim}R\operatorname{Hom}_B(K\otimes_AB,L\otimes_AB)
\]
is a quasi-isomorphism of underlying derived complexes of abelian groups (equivalently of $A$-modules by restriction on the right). In particular, for $A$-modules $M,N$ with $M$ $I$-power torsion, $\operatorname{Ext}_A^i(M,N)\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Ext}_B^i(M\otimes_AB,N\otimes_AB)$ for every $i\ge0$. Flatness allows ordinary tensor rather than derived tensor on modules.

records.title: Theorem — Injective embedding grothendieck

conclusions: Gorenstein at x iff f^!O_Y derived-invertible around x; locus open.
hypotheses: f flat in FTS_S, x∈X.
records.statement: A *Gorenstein local ring* is a Noetherian local ring of finite injective dimension as a module over itself; a scheme $T$ is *Gorenstein* if it is locally Noetherian and all its local rings are Gorenstein. A complex in $D(\mathcal O_T)$ is *derived-invertible* if it has a two-sided derived tensor inverse, equivalently it is locally a shift of a line bundle. For a scheme morphism $f:X\to Y$ whose fibres are locally Noetherian, *Gorenstein at $x$* means that $f$ is flat at $x$ and the local ring of $X_{f(x)}$ at $x$ is Gorenstein; *Gorenstein morphism* means this condition at every point. Fix a Noetherian scheme $S$ and the category $\mathrm{FTS}_S$ of separated finite-type $S$-schemes. For $f:X\to Y$ therein, let $f^!:D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}^+(\mathcal O_Y)\to D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}^+(\mathcal O_X)$ be the upper-shriek functor built from the right adjoint to proper pushforward on a compactification $X\hookrightarrow\bar X\to Y$. In particular $f^!\mathcal O_Y$ is a coherent bounded complex when $f$ is perfect. Let $f:X\to Y$ be flat in $\mathrm{FTS}_S$ and $x\in X$. Then $f$ is Gorenstein at $x$ iff there exists an open neighbourhood $U\subseteq X$ of $x$ on which $f^!\mathcal O_Y|_U$ is **derived-invertible**, i.e. locally isomorphic to a shift of a line bundle. In particular the pointwise Gorenstein locus is open. This relative criterion uses the upper-shriek *complex*, not just its zeroth cohomology.

Let $I$ be a directed preorder, $(X_i,f_{i'i}:X_{i'}\to X_i)$ an inverse system of schemes with $i'\ge i$, and $X=\varprojlim_i X_i$ with projections $f_i:X\to X_i$. Pullback produces a system $f_i^{-1}\mathcal F_i$ on $X$, whose *sheaf-colimit* is the sheafification of the sectionwise colimit. for all $p \geq 0$.

conclusions: \mathcal F is quasi-coherent.
\mathcal F is locally quasi-coherent and is a crystal in \mathcal O_{X/S}-modules.
hypotheses: Fix a prime $p$ and a divided power scheme $(S,\mathcal I,\gamma)$ over $\mathbf Z_{(p)}$, where $\mathcal I$ is a quasi-coherent ideal with divided powers. Set $S_0=V(\mathcal I)$ and choose a morphism $X\to S_0$ on which $p$ is locally nilpotent. A divided power thickening of $X/S$ is a triple $(U,T,\delta)$ with a closed immersion $U\hookrightarrow T$ inducing a homeomorphism on topological spaces, divided powers $\delta$ on its ideal $\mathcal J_T$, a compatible morphism of divided power schemes $T\to S$, and a map $U\to X$. These objects with compatible maps form $\mathrm{CRIS}(X/S)$; its full subcategory $\mathrm{Cris}(X/S)$ has $U\to X$ an open immersion. Both carry the Zariski topology (covers arise from Zariski covers of $T$ compatible with $U$). The forgetful functor $\mathrm{CRIS}(X/S)\to\operatorname{Sch}/X$ sends $(U,T,\delta)$ to $U$.

On the small crystalline site $\mathrm{Cris}(X/S)$, the crystalline structure sheaf $\mathcal O_{X/S}$ restricts to $\mathcal O_T$ on an object $(U,T,\delta)$. A sheaf $\mathcal F$ of $\mathcal O_{X/S}$-modules restricts to a sheaf $\mathcal F_T$ on $T$. It is a crystal if each pullback comparison map $f^*\mathcal F_T\to\mathcal F_{T'}$ for a morphism $(U',T',\delta')\to(U,T,\delta)$ is an isomorphism. It is locally quasi-coherent if every $\mathcal F_T$ is quasi-coherent, and quasi-coherent as a module on the site if it is locally presented by free $\mathcal O_{X/S}$-modules. The sheaf $\Omega_{X/S}$ is the universal divided power sheaf of differentials for the structure morphism of the crystalline site to the Zariski site of $S$; it restricts to $\Omega_{T/S,\delta}$ on each object.

These objects with compatible maps form $\mathrm{CRIS}(X/S)$; its full subcategory $\mathrm{Cris}(X/S)$ has $U\to X$ an open immersion. Both carry the Zariski topology (covers arise from Zariski covers of $T$ compatible with $U$). The forgetful functor $\mathrm{CRIS}(X/S)\to\operatorname{Sch}/X$ sends $(U,T,\delta)$ to $U$.

On the small crystalline site $\mathrm{Cris}(X/S)$, the crystalline structure sheaf $\mathcal O_{X/S}$ restricts to $\mathcal O_T$ on an object $(U,T,\delta)$. A sheaf $\mathcal F$ of $\mathcal O_{X/S}$-modules restricts to a sheaf $\mathcal F_T$ on $T$. It is a crystal if each pullback comparison map $f^*\mathcal F_T\to\mathcal F_{T'}$ for a morphism $(U',T',\delta')\to(U,T,\delta)$ is an isomorphism. It is locally quasi-coherent if every $\mathcal F_T$ is quasi-coherent, and quasi-coherent as a module on the site if it is locally presented by free $\mathcal O_{X/S}$-modules. The sheaf $\Omega_{X/S}$ is the universal divided power sheaf of differentials for the structure morphism of the crystalline site to the Zariski site of $S$; it restricts to $\Omega_{T/S,\delta}$ on each object.

Under the global crystalline setup above, let $\mathcal C=\mathrm{Cris}(X/S)$ or $\mathrm{CRIS}(X/S)$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of $\mathcal O_{X/S}$-modules on $\mathcal C$. The following are equivalent
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\mathcal{F}$ is quasi-coherent, and
\item $\mathcal{F}$ is locally quasi-coherent and a crystal in
$\mathcal{O}_{X/S}$-modules.
\end{enumerate}

For functions $f_1,\ldots,f_r$ on a ringed space, regular means successive multiplication maps on $\mathcal O/(f_1,\ldots,f_{i-1})$ are injective; no nonzero-final-quotient condition is imposed here. Koszul-regular means the Koszul complex has zero homology in every positive degree; $H_1$-regular means its degree-one homology vanishes; quasi-regular means, with $\mathcal J=(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$ the ideal sheaf generated by the sequence, that $(\mathcal O/\mathcal J)[T_1,\ldots,T_r]\to\bigoplus_{n\geq0}\mathcal J^n/\mathcal J^{n+1}$ is an isomorphism, sending $T_i$ to $f_i$ modulo $\mathcal J^2$. An ideal sheaf is of a given type if near each point of $\operatorname{Supp}(\mathcal O/\mathcal J)$ it admits generators of that type. For a ring regular sequence one additionally requires the final quotient nonzero. An immersion is of a given type when its defining ideal on an open where it is closed is of that type. Relative quasi/$H_1$-regular means also that its source is flat over the base. For an immersion $i:Z\to X$, choose an open $V\subset X$ where it is closed, with ideal $\mathcal I$; the conormal algebra $\mathcal C_{Z/X,*}$ has degree $n$ piece corresponding to $\mathcal I^n/\mathcal I^{n+1}$ on $Z$, and $\mathcal C_{Z/X}=\mathcal C_{Z/X,1}$. Assume $X$ is locally Noetherian.
The following are equivalent
\begin{enumerate}
\item $i$ is a regular immersion in a neighbourhood of $z$ and $j$
is a regular immersion in a neighbourhood of $y$,
\item $i$ and $j \circ i$ are regular immersions in a neighbourhood of $z$,
\item $j \circ i$ is a regular immersion in a neighbourhood of $z$ and the
conormal sequence
$$
0 \to i^*\mathcal{C}_{Y/X} \to
\mathcal{C}_{Z/X} \to
\mathcal{C}_{Z/Y} \to 0
$$
is split exact in a neighbourhood of $z$.
\end{enumerate}

For any $S$-scheme $T$ locally of finite type, write $\delta_T(t)=\delta(f(t))+\operatorname{trdeg}_{\kappa(f(t))}\kappa(t)$; for integral closed $W\subset T$, let $\dim_\delta W=\delta_T(\eta_W)$.

A $q$-cycle on $T$ is a locally finite integral linear combination of integral closed subschemes of $\delta$-dimension $q$; $Z_q(T)$ is the group of these cycles. For a closed subscheme $W$ of dimension at most $q$, $[W]_q$ is the sum of the $q$-dimensional components weighted by generic-point length multiplicities. The Chow group $\mathrm{CH}_q(T)$ is $Z_q(T)$ modulo rational equivalence generated by locally finite principal divisors on integral closed subschemes of dimension $q+1$.

For a nonzero meromorphic section $u$ of an invertible sheaf $\mathcal M$ on an integral scheme $W$, $\operatorname{div}_{\mathcal M}(u)$ is the Weil divisor with local coefficients given by the order of the representing meromorphic function in a trivialization at each codimension-one integral closed subscheme. Its Chow class is $c_1(\mathcal M)\cap[W]$. A global section $u$ has scheme-theoretic zero locus $Z(u)$. The operation $c_1(\mathcal M)\cap-:Z_q(T)\to\mathrm{CH}_{q-1}(T)$ is defined by restriction to each integral component $W$ and proper pushforward to $T$, and descends to Chow groups.

For a morphism $f:X\to Y$ and integer $p$, a bivariant class $c\in A^p(X\to Y)$ is a collection of homomorphisms $c_T:\mathrm{CH}_q(T)\to\mathrm{CH}_{q-p}(X\times_YT)$ indexed by $T\to Y$ and $q$, satisfying: (i) for proper $h:T'\to T$, $c_T(h_*\beta)=h_{X,*}c_{T'}(\beta)$; (ii) for flat $h$ of fixed relative dimension, $c_{T'}(h^*\alpha)=h_X^*c_T(\alpha)$; (iii) for $i:E\hookrightarrow T$ the zero scheme of a section of an invertible sheaf, $c_E(i^*\alpha)=i_X^*c_T(\alpha)$, with $h_X,i_X$ the base changes. Composition of families gives products $A^p(X\to Y)\times A^q(Y\to Z)\to A^{p+q}(X\to Z)$, and $A^*(X)=\bigoplus_pA^p(X\to X)$.

For a finite locally free sheaf $\mathcal E$ of rank $r$ on $X$, its operational Chern classes are $c_j(\mathcal E)\in A^j(X)$, with $c_0=1$, $c_j=0$ for $j>r$, and total class $c(\mathcal E)=\sum_jc_j(\mathcal E)$. Extend to general cycles by sum and proper pushforward, then to Chow groups.

hypotheses: Let $S$ be a scheme and $X$ an algebraic space over $S$. Write $|X|$ for its underlying topological space, obtained from the equivalence classes of morphisms $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ from spectra of fields. The fibre product of algebraic spaces is understood in the category of algebraic spaces. For an étale presentation $U\to X$ by a scheme, $R=U\times_XU$ is its groupoid of arrows with projections $s,t:R\rightrightarrows U$. A morphism is representable if every base change along a map from a scheme has scheme source.

For $x\in|X|$, condition $(\alpha)_x$ means every affine étale morphism $U\to X$ has only finitely many points over $x$. Condition $(\beta)_x$ means there is a monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ representing $x$. Condition $(\gamma)_x$ means there is a quasi-compact monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ representing $x$, equivalently for every affine étale $U\to X$ both fibres over $x$ of $|U|\to|X|$ and $|U\times_XU|\to|X|$ are finite. The conditions $(\alpha),(\beta),(\gamma)$ mean the corresponding pointwise property holds at every $x$.

An algebraic space $X$ is *decent* when it satisfies $(\gamma)$, equivalently every point $x$ can be represented by a quasi-compact monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)\to X$. It is *reasonable* when it satisfies $(\delta)$, equivalently the fibres of every affine étale presentation $U\to X$ are universally bounded. It is *very reasonable* when it satisfies $(\epsilon)$, equivalently it has a Zariski-local quasi-compact surjective étale cover by schemes. The implications scheme or quasi-separated $\Rightarrow$ very reasonable $\Rightarrow$ reasonable $\Rightarrow$ decent hold.

A *residual space* $Z_x\to X$ at $x\in|X|$ is the unique monomorphism from a reduced locally Noetherian algebraic space with singleton underlying topology whose image is $x$ and which is universal among morphisms of such spaces into $X$ representing $x$. A space is *locally separated* if its diagonal is an immersion; it is quasi-separated if its diagonal is quasi-compact and quasi-separated. A locally Noetherian algebraic space is one with an étale cover by locally Noetherian schemes.
